His 1960 visit to New York had already been a worldwide spectacle of speeches and theater. A return trip promised more of the same stagecraft. The short item tracks the early plans for that appearance.
cia-0000132678: Two items share a CIA paper dated March 2, 1961. The first reports Poland keeping up its long-term credits to Cuba. The second is item 6 of the Latin America series, cut short in the headline. Bloc credits were keeping the Cuban economy afloat through that winter. The short paper covers both halves as they were filed together that day.
cia-0000132778: Washington filed a third paper on Cuba and the Caribbean on August 4, 1960, and this briefing is that entry. Three same-day regional papers show a government watching closely, with Cuba at the center of its concerns. The declassified text survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive, cataloged as document 0000132778.
cia-0000135678: Dated 2 November 1960, this Spanish text is one of several 2506 Brigade documents bearing that same date in the declassified release. The brigade was a CIA-trained force of Cuban exiles preparing to land in Cuba. The catalog gives this item no distinguishing subject. Read together, the same-day papers suggest a busy administrative period in the camps; read alone, this one is a dated Spanish record of the brigade, preserved through the CIA Reading Room.
cia-0000135978: One declassified cable from the CIA files, dated 1 February 1954, covers the trading of a burnt plane, raised as a possibility in a cable from the Lincoln station. Lincoln was where PBSUCCESS staff worked the Guatemala operation day to day, under code names, in 1953 and 1954. Nothing in the heading promises drama, yet the sheet adds one more firm date and subject to the coup record.
cia-0000136278: A cable of 1 May 1954 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with Instruction 15 for broadcast, the high-water mark of the numbered script series. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000138978: Russian troop disposition is the subject of this 1946 report. The sample kept here is mostly markings. Distribution stamps limit it to American and British officials. Report numbers and dates fill the rest. The troop data itself does not appear in readable form. No honest summary of unit locations can be given. The entry's value is as an artifact. It shows early Cold War order-of-battle reporting. Its substance stays locked in the original file.
cia-03179878: April 15, 1955: the day's intelligence went out. Analysts sent their global roundup to senior officials. The Cold War's tax-day brief. Future scholars will discover it. This declassified bulletin stays. It is archived. Time has kept the file intact.
cia-06485478: 1. <SANITIZED> REPORTS THAT THE ASSASSINATION OF DR. MARTIN LUTHER KING, a CIA document. The King assassination file. This file preserves that declassified paper. The paper lived through the years. Later readers can locate it. The paper lasts as a quiet witness to its time.
cia-06569678: SLOBODAN MILOSEVIC - "FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF YUGOSLAVIA", a CIA document. The Serbian leader's file. This file preserves that declassified paper. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cia-06712178: CARTEL/HUNTER TEAM, a CIA document. The team file. This file preserves that declassified paper. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
cia-06795978: WEST GERMANY - USSR NEW STRAINS AFTER CHERNOBYL, a CIA document. The post-disaster strains. This file preserves that declassified paper. History keeps its place secure. Such papers rarely see the light of day. The paper lived through the years.
davila-civil-wars-of-france-1678:
Enrico Caterino Davila, an Italian soldier who served at the side of Henri IV, wrote his Historia delle guerre civili di Francia in 1630. The English translation by Charles Cotterell and William Aylesbury, first made in 1647, appears here in the 1678 printing. Davila had seen the French wars of religion as a young man in the king's service.

His history covers the long struggle between crown, Catholics, and Huguenots that tore France apart. He writes as both witness and analyst, weighing causes with a soldier's knowledge of camps and courts. The book became the classic near-contemporary history of those wars. Its balance and detail kept it in readers' hands for two centuries.
doe-osti-3367768-final-report-for-doe-sc: SC0022078 got finally reported, and this DOE final covers the report. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was final. The closeout was researcher. The SC0022078 were final. The DOE were report. The researchers were closeout.
doe-osti-3626688-final-technical-report-: DE-SC0023178 got technical-finalled, and this DOE final covers the report. The pages detail the final findings. The researchers get their closeout. The report was technical. The closeout was researcher. The DE-SC0023178 were report. The technical were closeout.
ebers-egypt-descriptive-vol-1-1878:
Georg Ebers showed Egypt to the crowd in Vol. 1 of Egypt: Descriptive, Historical, and Picturesque, out in English in 1878. Ebers was both a sage of Egypt and a famed tale smith. Clara Bell turned his German text to English. Great draws fill the tome: the Nile, Cairo, the heaps, and the shrines in rich, warm views.

Text and draw blend to teach as they charm. Crowds in its age learned their Egypt from these pages first. The pair of tomes was the most loved drawn guide of its time. This tome starts the tour.
ebers-egypt-descriptive-vol-2-1878:
Georg Ebers takes the tour up the Nile in Vol. 2 of Egypt: Descriptive, Historical, and Picturesque, out in English in 1878. The first tome gave the north and the great heaps. Here the trek runs south: Luxor, Karnak, the tombs of kings, and isles in the stream, all in the rich draws that made the set a craze in its age.

Ebers knew the land as a sage and loved it as a tale smith. Clara Bell's English prose keeps that warmth. The tome ends the most loved drawn guide of its time. Its charm still works.
europmc-pmc10242978:
Wang and colleagues test whether ferroptosis inducers can strengthen copper-driven cell death in liver cancer, in a 2023 study. Cuproptosis and ferroptosis are two newly defined forms of cell death, one driven by copper and one by iron. How the two pathways interact was unclear when the team began.

They treated liver cancer cells with copper-carrying drugs plus ferroptosis inducers. The combination killed more cancer cells than either approach alone in their tests. The study suggests that pairing metal-based death pathways could yield a stronger treatment for a stubborn cancer.
europmc-pmc10247378:
Martínez-Jiménez and colleagues compare the whole genomes of primary and metastatic solid tumors across many cancer types, in a 2023 study. Cancer that has spread, called metastatic cancer, is what usually kills patients. Yet most genome studies sample early tumors before spread, so the changes that come with spread were poorly mapped.

The team compared thousands of tumor genomes from both stages. They describe which changes appear early and which arise or grow during spread and treatment. The map helps explain how cancers advance and where new treatments might intervene.
europmc-pmc10281978:
Yan and colleagues report that the level of a cystine transporter called SLC7A11 decides how cancer cells answer oxidative stress, in a 2023 study. The transporter shields cancer cells from stress and is found at high levels in many tumors. The team expected more of it to always mean more protection, and found something stranger.

Moderate excess of the transporter helped cancer cells, as expected. Very high levels instead made cells fragile under stress in their tests. The surprise finding reshapes how researchers think about targeting this common cancer shield.
europmc-pmc10772178:
Zhang and co-authors reviewed ischemia-reperfusion injury in 2024, the harm that strikes when blood flow returns. A cut in flow starves tissue; its return can then deepen the damage. The Wnt signal path, a web that steers cell fate, threads through that harm. It cross-talks with many other paths in the web.

One branch of Wnt aids organ recovery, Zhang reports. The other branches make the injury worse. The paths jointly steer cell death, swelling, vessel growth, and scarring. Brain harm and a leaky brain barrier form part of the map too. The review sorts care ideas by which branch they move. Proof spans animal work, care standards, and patient trials.
europmc-pmc1088278:
Nielsen and co-authors scanned human and chimp genes for signs of rapid, favoured change in this 2005 study. Humans and chimps split about five million years ago and differ sharply in body and mind. Their DNA, though, differs only a little. The team compared 13,731 genes between the two species to find ones shaped by positive selection, where helpful changes spread fast.

Genes for smell, taste, and immune defence often carried the signal, they found. So did genes that suppress tumours, control cell death, and aid sperm making, which surprised the team. Brain genes showed little sign of such selection, while testis genes showed a lot. Genes on the X chromosome also stood out. The authors offer gene variant data for the top 50 genes as a resource.
europmc-pmc11219878:
Zhu, Chen, Masson, and Li review the signals that turn stem cells into bone-forming cells in this 2024 paper. Osteoblasts are the cells that build bone. They arise when mesenchymal stem cells, a flexible adult stem cell type, commit to the bone lineage. That commitment is governed by signal pathways and by gene-switch proteins.

Ten pathways are detailed, among them Wnt, BMP, TGF-beta, Hedgehog, and Notch. Key gene switches include Runx2, Osterix, ATF4, and SATB2. Hormones add a further layer of control over the process. Epigenetic factors, which tune gene use without altering DNA, also play critical roles. The review synthesises the latest work on each layer. The authors aim to clarify how commitment, differentiation, bone formation, and upkeep are regulated as one system.
europmc-pmc11542778:
Cross, Choma, and Onofrey examine bias in medical AI and its clinical consequences in this 2024 paper. Biases arise and compound throughout the AI lifecycle, from data collection to publication. In tools that guide clinical decisions, biased output can mean substandard care. It can also perpetuate and worsen longstanding healthcare disparities.

The authors walk through bias at each stage: data and labels, model building, testing, rollout, and publication. Small sample sizes for certain patient groups yield weak performance and clinically empty predictions for them. Missing data bias behaviour too, including diagnosis codes missing non-randomly and social determinants of health that are rarely captured. Labels annotated by experts may carry their hidden biases. The paper maps each trap so developers can design against it.
europmc-pmc1318478:
Bordone and co-authors linked an aging gene to insulin release in mice in 2006. Sirt1 is the mammal version of a known aging pathway gene. Pancreatic beta cells store and release insulin. The team tested whether Sirt1 controls that release.

Sirt1 boosted insulin secretion by repressing a gene called UCP2. It binds the UCP2 promoter directly to quiet it. Cutting Sirt1 raised UCP2 and blunted insulin output. Cells then failed to raise energy currency after glucose. Removing UCP2 restored secretion despite low Sirt1. Food deprivation also raised UCP2 in mouse pancreas.
europmc-pmc1331978:
Maksakova and co-authors reviewed retroviral elements and mouse mutations in 2006. The lab mouse is a core model for human biology. Its mutation pattern differs sharply from the human one. Transposable element insertions cause about 0.1 percent of new human mutations.

In mice the figure runs one hundred times higher. Active endogenous retroviruses drive that ongoing activity. Insertions alter gene expression and create varied mutations. The review covers how these elements interact with host cells. Maksakova argues the mouse genome is still losing its arms race against invaders. It appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2006. Mice and men share most genes, but not these rates of change.
europmc-pmc2062478:
Begun and a large team sequenced whole genomes of the fruit fly Drosophila simulans in 2007. They used shotgun sequencing of several inbred lines. Comparing variation within the species with differences from two close relatives shows how natural selection shapes genomes. The relatives were Drosophila melanogaster and Drosophila yakuba. Their goal was a population-level view of polymorphism and divergence.

They found large, previously unknown swings in variation and divergence along chromosome arms. The X chromosome carried less variation and diverged faster than other chromosomes. The team listed functional genome elements shaped by adaptive evolution. They also mapped base composition patterns in coding and non-coding DNA. The data set offers a rich resource for studying adaptation and functional variation in this species.
europmc-pmc2098778:
Cho reviewed cancer-linked microRNAs, called oncomiRs, in 2007. MicroRNAs are tiny RNA molecules, about 22 units long, that regulate genes after they are copied. Some drive cancer growth, while others suppress it. The review covers their discovery, how they act on target messages, and their use in diagnosis and prognosis across human cancers.

Several examples show the range of effects. MiR-15 and miR-16 trigger cell death by targeting the survival gene Bcl2. The miR-17-92 cluster promotes tumour formation through the gene E2F1. MiR-34a suppresses nerve tumour growth by lowering E2F3 protein. Chromosome swaps in tumours can free the growth gene HMGA2 from let-7 control. Profiling oncomiR patterns in cancers has also produced diagnostic and prognostic signatures, patterns that help classify disease and predict outcome.
europmc-pmc2124878: A medical paper on the bacteriology of sputum in non-tuberculous upper airway infections. The coughed germs. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125178: A medical paper on the mechanism of anaphylatoxin formation in ferment action. The shock poison. This article preserves that immunology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125278: A medical paper on reactions between bacteria and animal tissues under artificial conditions. The germs meet flesh. This article preserves that bacteriology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2125378: A medical paper on the influence upon tadpoles of feeding desiccated thyroid gland. The thyroid-fed tadpoles. This article preserves that endocrinology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125478: A medical paper on the relation between the thyroid and parathyroid glands. The neck glands' kinship. This article preserves that endocrinology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2130978: A medical paper with studies on urobilin physiology and pathology, pigment absorption. The bile pigment. This article preserves that physiology. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
europmc-pmc2131078: A medical paper on tissue changes following deprivation of fat-soluble A vitamin. The vitamin-starved flesh. This article preserves that nutrition research. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2131278: A medical paper with studies on a paratyphoid infection in guinea pigs, factors involved. The guinea pig typhoid. This article preserves that bacteriology. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. The library keeps the document safe for everyone.
europmc-pmc2140578: A biology paper on circus movements of Limulus and the tropism theory. The horseshoe crab's circles. This article preserves that zoology. It awaits future readers. It holds its historical place. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2206478:
Bozza and colleagues profiled blood cytokines in severe sepsis patients in 2007, hunting for markers of severity. Sepsis is a whole-body response to infection that can fail organs and kill. Doctors lack accurate, quick biomarkers to group patients by risk. The team studied 60 patients in four tertiary hospitals. A multiplex assay measured 17 cytokines, immune signalling proteins, in each blood sample at once.

Nine cytokines, including IL-6, IL-8 and IL-10, ran significantly higher in septic shock than in severe sepsis without shock. IL-8 and MCP-1 tracked organ failure scores best on day one. IL-6, IL-8 and G-CSF levels in the first 24 hours predicted whether organ failure would worsen by day three. Several cytokines predicted early death well. In adjusted analysis, only MCP-1 independently predicted prognosis.
europmc-pmc2435278:
Xi, Ramirez, and Dimopoulos studied how the dengue mosquito fights the virus it carries in 2008. Aedes aegypti spreads dengue fever to humans, yet the mosquito itself resists the virus with its innate immune system. Working from the newly read mosquito genome, the team combined gene activity scans with gene-silencing tests.

One defence pathway, the Toll pathway, stood out as a real controller of dengue infection. Several Toll-linked genes changed activity after infection, and silencing pathway parts altered how well the virus did. The mosquito's natural gut microbes also mattered. They appeared to keep the Toll pathway lightly primed, so infected mosquitoes with normal microbes resisted better. The authors said this is the first full account of this mosquito's anti-dengue defence, distinct from the fruit fly systems studied before.
europmc-pmc2553778:
Redmond, Crane, and Menz established reference values in 2008 for the Foot Posture Index, a clinical score of how a standing foot is shaped. Clinicians use the index to classify foot type, but no normal ranges existed to judge a score against. The authors pooled raw data from nine research groups, totalling 1,648 observations, and derived norms from the healthy subset.

A slightly pronated foot, rolling gently inward, proved to be the normal resting posture, with an average score of plus 4. Scores followed a U-shape with age: children and older adults scored higher than mid-life adults. Sex made no difference, and body mass index showed no link to the score. Patients with high-arched feet from nerve or unknown causes scored clearly apart from the norms.
europmc-pmc2564978:
Ji and colleagues tested in 2008 whether restoring a small RNA called miR-34 could tame stomach cancer cells that had lost p53, a master tumour suppressor. MiR-34 normally works downstream of p53, and it targets genes that help cancer stem cells renew themselves and survive. The team put miR-34 back into Kato III gastric cancer cells, which carry mutant p53, and measured the effects.

Restoration lowered the target proteins Bcl-2, Notch, and HMGA2. Cells grew more slowly, stalled in the G1 resting phase, and showed more activation of caspase-3, an executioner of cell suicide. They also became more sensitive to chemotherapy when their Bcl-2 level was high. Most strikingly, treated cells largely lost the ability to form tumorspheres, the floating balls that signal stem-like self-renewal.
europmc-pmc2629778:
Corander, Marttinen, Sirén, and Tang introduced enhanced statistical tools in 2008 for their BAPS software, which infers the genetic structure of populations. Bayesian methods in BAPS sort individuals into genetic clusters, but rising data volumes and more complex questions were outgrowing the existing models. The new version adds an array of modelling options.

Users can now fit mixture models with a chosen number of clusters. They can also estimate interbreeding, called admixture, under a model that respects genetic linkage. Linkage is the tendency of nearby variants to travel together. The software can flag alleles in an individual that come from a different ancestry than the surrounding genome. It also lets researchers compare pre-specified hypotheses about population structure directly using Bayes' theorem. Computations can now be spread across several computers through a script interface.
europmc-pmc2644678:
Eden and colleagues presented in 2009 a free web tool, called GOrilla, that helps biologists make sense of long ranked lists of genes. Modern experiments often rank thousands of genes, for example by how much their activity changed. The Gene Ontology is a standard set of labels for gene jobs, and the question is which jobs cluster near the top of a list.

Older tools forced users to split their list into a chosen set and a background set first. GOrilla skips that step and scans the whole ranking directly. Its math gives an exact measure of how unlikely each cluster is by chance, without slow trial runs. Results come back as a tree diagram that shows how the winning labels relate to each other. A full scan of thousands of genes takes only seconds.
europmc-pmc2654478:
Vlachos and fellow specialists issued shared guidance in 2008 on Diamond Blackfan anaemia, a rare inherited failure to make red blood cells. The Participants of Sixth Annual Daniella Maria Arturi International Consensus Conference met to settle how the disease should be found and treated. It strikes about seven babies per million, usually in the first year of life.

The disease stems from early red cell makers that die too readily, and it often comes with birth defects and a raised cancer risk. The group reviewed the three main treatments: steroid drugs, regular blood transfusions, and stem cell transplants. They set out who should get which option, and how care should be planned over a lifetime. Because the disease is rare, much advice rests on expert judgment rather than trials, which the authors state plainly.
europmc-pmc2695778:
Lindgren and colleagues, with the Giant Consortium and partner groups, merged 16 genome studies in 2009 to find genes controlling where the body stores fat. Belly fat matters more for diabetes and heart disease than total weight, yet its genetics lagged behind. The combined scan covered 38,580 adults measured for waist size and waist-to-hip ratio.

Twenty-six candidate variants went forward for checking in up to 70,689 more people. Three regions confirmed. Two, near genes called TFAP2B and MSRA, moved waist size, apparently through overall fatness. The third, near LYPLAL1, shifted waist-to-hip ratio in women only, a pure fat-distribution effect. The split is the point: some genes make people fatter, while others decide where the fat goes, and the second kind can harm even at the same total weight.
europmc-pmc2714578:
Wassmer and co-authors mapped in 2009 how the retromer complex, a protein coat that sorts cargo inside cells, links sorting to transport. Retromer pulls chosen cargo from early endosomes, small sorting sacs, back to the trans-Golgi network, a shipping hub. Mammals were known to use several sorting nexins, proteins that bend membranes, but how they paired up stayed unclear.

They found four mammalian retromers, each with a distinct mix of sorting nexins one, two, five, and six. Two nexins bind the dynactin activator of dynein, a motor that hauls cargo along cell tracks, which sets the layout of the network. Another nexin binds a tether at the Golgi hub, which completes the route.
europmc-pmc2736378:
Welch and co-authors tested in 2009 which design choices control how much protein a synthetic gene makes in E. coli bacteria. Synthetic genes are now a standard route to make therapeutic and research proteins, but redesign rules rested on little direct evidence. They synthesized two sets of forty genes for two valuable proteins, varying only in synonymous codons, alternate spellings for the same building block.

Protein output ranged from undetectable to thirty percent of all cell protein, driven strongly by codons for a subset of amino acids. Favorable codons were those read by transfer RNAs that stay most charged during amino acid starvation, not the codons commonest in highly expressed native genes. New genes designed by their model performed as predicted.
europmc-pmc2745878:
Terwilliger described in 2003 an automated method for building protein models. It builds the main chain into an X-ray electron-density map. It works by template matching and iterative fragment extension. Model building is the first reading of the map in terms of atom positions, and at low resolution errors are hard for later refinement to fix. Manual building can take a day or far longer when maps are unclear.

The method finds likely helices, strands, and other fragments by matching templates against the map, then extends fragments step by step to trace the chain. It builds on earlier tracing and fragment-fitting methods but automates the search decisions. Faster automated building speeds the whole structure determination process, especially for difficult, low-resolution cases.
europmc-pmc2760878:
Wu and Eisen presented AMPHORA in 2008, an automated pipeline for phylogenomic inference that builds organism trees from many protein markers at once. Microbial classification long rested on a single ribosomal RNA gene, the gold standard, yet single genes can misplace distant organisms due to composition bias. Whole genomes now supply every protein gene, but cloning and aligning many markers by hand was slow.

AMPHORA automates marker choice, alignment, and tree building for large data sets, using protein sequences that are less prone to nucleotide bias. It lets researchers corroborate ribosomal trees with genome-wide evidence at scale. The pipeline aims to make robust, multi-gene phylogeny a routine step in microbial systematics and ecology rather than a bespoke effort.
europmc-pmc2816178:
Thornton and Woods reviewed primary microcephaly in 2009, an inherited condition where the brain grows far too small before birth while its structure stays normal. Studying it offers a clean window on how the fetal brain builds its outer layer, the cerebral cortex, which is unusually large in humans.

Eight gene locations and five genes had been pinned to the condition when the review was written. Surprisingly, every known protein from those genes spends part of the cell cycle at the centrosome, a hub that organizes cell division. One gene, ASPM, accounts for about half of all cases. The authors argue the centrosome acts as a meeting point where many control pathways for early brain growth converge.
europmc-pmc2848978:
Hackl, Grillari, and a large team hunted in 2010 for microRNAs, tiny gene regulators, that change consistently as human cells age. Single studies had tied scattered microRNAs to aging, but no shared signature had emerged. The team profiled seven aging models: four cell types aged in dishes, plus foreskin, stem cells, and immune cells taken from young and old donors.

Four microRNAs fell across nearly every model. MiR-17 dropped in all seven, and three close relatives dropped in most. As they fell, some of their target genes rose, notably p21, a brake on cell division long tied to cell aging. The authors propose the four as shared markers of human cellular aging.
europmc-pmc2868878:
Slater, Spanlang, Sanchez-Vives, and Blanke showed in 2010 that a person can feel a virtual body as their own without any matching touch. Earlier illusions, like the rubber hand trick, needed touch seen and felt at the same moment. Here men put on immersive virtual reality and saw a life-sized female body from its own viewpoint, standing where their body should be.

That first-person view alone created a strong sense of owning the virtual body, reported on questionnaires. When the virtual body was threatened, the men's heart rates slowed in the classic fear response, as if their own body were at risk. The result shows vision from inside a body can outweigh touch cues, and it gives science a tool for probing how the brain builds the sense of self.
europmc-pmc2873978:
Patel, Bhattacharya, and Butte ran in 2010 a scan of the environment for type 2 diabetes modeled on genome-wide scans. Instead of testing genes one study at a time, they tested two hundred sixty-six measured exposures, from nutrients to pollutants, against diabetes in national survey cohorts. Diabetes status came from fasting blood sugar, and models adjusted for age, sex, weight, ethnicity, and income level.

Two signals survived strict checks and repeated in separate cohorts. A breakdown product of the banned pesticide heptachlor raised the odds of diabetes notably per step up in exposure. A form of vitamin E called gamma-tocopherol also tracked higher odds, a surprise for a nutrient often seen as protective. The pilot proved the scan approach can flag overlooked environmental suspects.
europmc-pmc2936378:
Van Herck and co-authors systematically reviewed pay-for-performance schemes in health care in a 2010 article, gathering studies published over roughly two decades. Such schemes pay doctors or hospitals extra for meeting quality targets and vary widely in design.

More than a hundred evaluation studies offered a large but cautious body of evidence, strongest for clinical quality and fairness of care. Far less was known about teamwork, patient focus, or value for money. Results hinged on how schemes were built and on local context. The review maps which design choices seem to help or hinder.
europmc-pmc2944278:
Agusti and the ECLIPSE investigators described the wide variety of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a 2010 cohort study. The lung condition mixes airway damage with problems elsewhere in the body, and patients differ greatly.

Over two thousand stable patients were compared with smokers whose lungs tested normal and with people who never smoked. Patients carried more other illnesses than controls at every severity stage. Standard airflow grades matched poorly with breathlessness, exercise ability, flare-ups, and general health, and values spread widely within each grade. Even severe airflow blockage sometimes came with few symptoms, underlining the condition's patchwork nature.
europmc-pmc3014878:
Szarka and colleagues ran a 2010 study of immune signal molecules in blood. They compared healthy pregnancies with preeclampsia. That dangerous complication of pregnancy is marked by body-wide inflammation. Single markers had given a patchy picture.

Sixty patients, sixty healthy pregnant women, and about sixty non-pregnant controls were compared using a multiplex array plus targeted tests. Normal pregnancy already shifted the circulating mix, and preeclampsia shifted it further in characteristic directions. The team related the patterns to clinical features and to markers of vessel activation, oxidative stress, and debris from the placenta.
europmc-pmc3044678:
Wang and coauthors tested in 2011 whether the switch from juvenile to adult growth in trees uses the same small RNA controls known from small annual plants. In annuals, one tiny RNA is high in seedlings and falls as the plant matures, while a second rises. The team tracked both RNAs in several woody species with clear young and adult forms, including eucalyptus, acacia, ivy, and oak.

The same opposing pattern appeared in the trees. Forcing a poplar hybrid to keep making the juvenile RNA held back its target genes and the adult RNA, and the trees stayed juvenile far longer than normal. The result shows the phase change clock is shared across plant lineages that split long ago. Breeders and foresters who need to speed or delay maturity can use that shared switch as a handle.
europmc-pmc3252278:
Hisato Kobayashi and colleagues produced single-letter-resolution maps of DNA methylation in mouse eggs and sperm, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Genetics. Methylation patterns are rewritten in the germline and carry imprinting, the parent-of-origin marks that control some genes. Using whole-genome bisulfite sequencing alongside RNA sequencing, the team compared the two gametes directly.

The maps turned out strikingly different. In eggs, methylation tracked with gene activity, concentrating in the bodies of active genes. In sperm, methylation covered nearly everything except CpG-rich islands, and promoter methylation ran opposite to expression. The comparison found over sixteen hundred regions methylated differently between egg and sperm, beyond the known imprinting control regions, and about half resisted the wiping that follows fertilization. Most egg-specific marks needed the protein Dnmt3L, splitting egg methylation into two functional types.
europmc-pmc3306778:
Kool led an international team that pooled data on a childhood brain tumor called medulloblastoma, reporting in 2012. It is the most common malignant brain tumor of childhood, yet studies disagreed on how many distinct kinds exist. Gene based work suggested the tumor is really several diseases wearing one name, so the team merged results from seven studies covering hundreds of tumors.

The combined data support exactly four core subgroups, labeled WNT, SHH, Group 3, and Group 4. Each group differs sharply in gene activity, DNA changes, patient age and sex patterns, and survival chances. A second large group of tumors, sorted with a simpler tissue test, gave nearly the same picture. The authors say future trials should treat and study each subgroup on its own terms.
europmc-pmc3320478:
Hayes led a companion review on how West Nile virus spreads and circulates, published in 2005. Since its 1999 arrival in New York, the virus had caused more than sixteen thousand reported cases in the United States. Birds carry the virus in their blood, and Culex mosquitoes pick it up and pass it to people, horses, and other animals.

The review explains what drives the intensity of spread in a place, from mosquito numbers and feeding habits to local weather and human behavior. Reported infection rates in hard hit neighborhoods were surprisingly low, meaning whole populations remain vulnerable in later seasons. Rarer routes, including blood transfusion, organ transplants, and infection before birth, are also covered. The authors gather the first five years of Western Hemisphere experience into one account of the virus's ecology.
europmc-pmc3346778:
Braun and colleagues tested how steady urine markers of two common chemical exposures are across pregnancy, in a 2012 study. Phthalates, used in plastics and personal care products, and bisphenol A, used in can linings and plastics, may affect mother and child health. Most studies measure them once, in a single urine sample, which is only fair if levels hold steady over time.

The team collected over a thousand samples from one hundred thirty seven women, before and during pregnancy. Average levels looked similar in both periods, but steadiness varied sharply by chemical. Two phthalate markers were moderately stable, so one sample sorted women's exposure reasonably well. Bisphenol A and several other markers swung widely, meaning one sample can badly misclassify exposure. The authors advise repeat sampling for the jumpier chemicals in pregnancy research.
europmc-pmc3366978:
Linden and colleagues piloted a therapy in which people with depression learn to regulate their own emotion circuits using real-time brain scanning. Many patients respond incompletely to drugs or talking therapy, so the team tested whether neurofeedback from functional MRI could add a self-directed route to improvement.

Eight patients completed four neurofeedback sessions, learning to boost activity in areas involved in positive emotion, including the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex and insula, while viewing their own brain signals. Their scores on a standard depression rating scale improved significantly. A comparison group using the same mental strategies without feedback did not improve. The authors call for blinded randomised trials to rule out placebo effects.
europmc-pmc3373078:
Chadha and colleagues reported in 2006 that Nipah virus had caused a 2001 outbreak of brain fever in Siliguri, India. The virus had never been detected in India before. Patients in four hospitals, their family contacts, and medical staff fell ill with fever and confusion during January and February of that year.

Tests at the time found no culprit, and Japanese encephalitis was first blamed. Years later, stored samples were checked because the Siliguri cases resembled Nipah outbreaks in nearby Bangladesh. The re-analysis linked the outbreak to Nipah, a bat-borne virus that killed a large share of its victims elsewhere. The finding extended the virus's known map into India.
europmc-pmc3482178:
Keshari and co-authors studied how inflammatory signals push white blood cells to cast out DNA traps, in a 2012 PLoS ONE paper. The traps, webs of DNA and germ-killing proteins, catch microbes but can also harm tissue. The team worked with patients who had a whole-body inflammatory state, a dangerous condition that can follow injury or infection even without germs.

Blood from those patients carried more trap material, and their isolated cells made extra traps and reactive chemicals. Plasma from patients made healthy cells do the same. Three inflammatory signals drove the effect, and blocking them cut trap release. Keshari's group shows these signals act through two enzymes in the cells. The chain helps explain tissue damage in severe inflammation.

frus-1861-d178:
A letter of 3 September 1861 went from William H. Seward to Carl Schurz in Madrid. The letter is document 178 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

September orders to Spain dealt with the watch on ports and trade. Cuba's harbors lay close to the blockade's edge. Seward's letter kept Schurz alert to any Spanish step that might let Southern ships find shelter or supplies. Cuba's governor took orders from Madrid, which made Schurz's post a guard on the island too. A guard on the island, kept by letter, cost the Union no ships at all.
frus-1861-d278:
News and judgment from Mr. Angel reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 10 June 1861. It was printed as Document 278 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. It was written in the opening months of the Civil War, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1861-d78:
Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 9 September 1861. The dispatch is document 78 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two Adams letters in three days mark a full week at the London post. Notes, calls, and press talk filled the envoy's days. The second letter shows how fast fresh points could pile up, each one needing a clear report home. Fast work in September kept the small points from growing into open quarrels. Small points, met fast, stayed small; that was the whole art of the autumn.
frus-1862-d178:
On 30 October 1862 Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London, in a report printed as Document 178 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of two Adams letters under that date.

The end of October found the French plan for a joint truce proposal nearly ready, while Britain hung back. Adams's reports from these days are prized because he heard British doubts at close range. This letter forms part of the closing record of October, the month when European action on the war came closest and then began to recede. Earl Russell, the British foreign secretary, was the minister Adams dealt with most in London.
frus-1862-d278:
Dated 12 May 1862, Document 278 is a dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward to William L. Dayton, the American minister in Paris. It is printed in the France section of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

By mid-May, France was digesting its check at Puebla and reinforcing its army in Mexico. Washington saw a chance: a France busy in Mexico might think twice about the Confederacy. Seward's letters of this period, this one among them, probed that opening while keeping formal ties smooth with the French government. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d378: A translated paper dated 19 September 1862 stands as Document 378 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Filed in the French section between letters of Viscount Treilhard and Secretary Seward. The heading marks it only as a translation, with no author or reader named. So the entry rests on its date, its form, and its place in that file.
frus-1862-d478:
On 11 August 1862 James E. Harvey reported from Lisbon to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 478 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Harvey wrote in the weeks when the Confederate cruiser Alabama had just slipped to sea and begun her raids. Portuguese waters, including the Azores, were among the places such ships might use. A report from Lisbon in that month spoke directly to the Union's effort against the raiders. The Union hoped to hem them in by law. It could not reach them by force. Harvey's letters give the State Department's side of that effort, from one of the ports where it was actually decided.
frus-1862-d578:
On 23 July 1862 James Watson Webb reported from Rio de Janeiro to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is Document 578 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed for Congress.

Webb's July reports came as the war at sea was spreading south in prospect. Confederate cruisers were fitting out to raid American commerce. Their hunting ground would be the ocean routes. Brazil's many ports could shelter such ships or shut them out, depending on the rules Rio enforced. A minister's report on Brazilian intentions was therefore practical intelligence, not ceremony. The letter belongs to the maritime side of the volume, where the Union fought to turn neutral law into a wall around its merchant fleet.
frus-1862-d678:
Anson Burlingame wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 24 July 1862. The dispatch comes from Burlingame's post as American minister to China. It is document 678 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, in the heart of the summer mail.

Summer letters from China brought word on trade and on the Qing court's long fight with the Taiping revolt. Burlingame's reports also served Americans who lived and traded in the treaty ports, whose safety rested on his work. This dispatch is one of the last in his 1862 run, and it shows an envoy settled into the rhythm of a hard, distant post.
frus-1862-d78:
In a letter dated 9 June 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 78 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. The date falls in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1863p1-d178:
A dispatch dated 1 May 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 178 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

The CSS Alabama, built in a British yard, had escaped to sea in 1862 and was burning Union merchant ships. London's handling of such ships hung over every report Adams sent home. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d278: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 3 September 1863. It is document 278 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d378:
Writing in Washington on 30 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 378 in the 1863 volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Taken as a run, these notes chart Britain slowly accepting that the Union would not collapse. That judgment, formed in Washington, helped keep Britain out of the war. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d478:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 25 April 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d578:
Secretary William H. Seward addressed a formal note to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 25 June 1863. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. The letter is one piece of the steady stream of notes that passed between the two governments in the early summer of 1863.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d678:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams, his minister in London, on 30 November 1863. The letter appears as document 678 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863. Adams was the main American voice in Britain through the whole Civil War.

The Union's great fear was that Britain might back the South or treat it as a full nation. Seward's London mail worked against that risk day after day. This dispatch is one small part of that steady push. Read with its neighbors, it helps show how talks stayed open and calm even while a hard war went on at home.
frus-1863p1-d78:
Charles Francis Adams wrote this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 13 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 78 in part one of the 1863 volume.

A three-letter day at the legation meant a full plate: talks, papers, and people to report on. Adams kept each sheet to its own head, a habit that makes his file easy to read still. This one opens the set of 13 February. In a volume built from such days, it is one more proof of the post's pace at the heart of the war.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d178: American delegation minutes of the final meeting of the Moscow Conference, held on October 30, 1943, form Document 178 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The final session sealed three weeks of talks and set the texts the ministers signed that day. Minutes of a closing meeting carry the formal end of a story the letters in this volume tell in pieces. The volume prints them in the Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d278:
A long Cairo meeting of 26 November 1943 left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The Log dates the start at half past four, but other accounts suggest it ran at least two hours, with Churchill and the Chiangs at Roosevelt's villa for much of the afternoon.

Elliott Roosevelt describes a final political conference in the garden, with Harriman, Eden, and Cadogan present, framing the words of the Cairo communiqué. For security, that statement was held back until after Tehran, and until Stalin approved its text. Stilwell's account adds that Chiang agreed to Burma points he had rejected the day before. The note closes with a long list of other Roosevelt-Chiang topics, from a billion-dollar loan to the Chengtu airfield costs.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d378:
Charles Bohlen's minutes record a private talk between President Roosevelt and Marshal Stalin at Tehran on 1 December 1943, at twenty past three. Roosevelt had asked Stalin to come to him to speak briefly and frankly, and the subject was American domestic politics.

Roosevelt explains that an election falls in 1944, that he may have to run again if the war continues. Six or seven million Americans of Polish descent must not be lost as voters. Personally he favors moving Poland's eastern border west and her western border to the Oder, but he cannot join any decision at Tehran or speak publicly now. On the Baltic states, he jokes he will not go to war when Soviet armies reoccupy them, but asks for some public expression of the people's will in time. Stalin answers that chances for that will come under the Soviet constitution, with no international control.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d478:
A further memorandum by the United States Chiefs of Staff bears the date December 4, 1943, the first day of the Second Cairo Conference. The American chiefs were pressing to convert the broad Tehran understandings into fixed plans. The State Department included the paper in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Written positions mattered at Cairo because the two allies still differed over the balance between the cross-Channel attack and operations in the Mediterranean. The American chiefs stated their case in papers like this before arguing it in session. For readers, the memorandum is evidence from inside that argument, showing how the United States framed its demands at the summit's military level.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d78: Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek on October 30, 1943, his second letter to China's leader in four days. It is Document 78 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The Cairo meeting, where Chiang would sit with Roosevelt and Churchill, was now set for late November, and the letters of these weeks arranged it. The record gives the date and the names. The text in the Foreign Relations series holds the details.
frus-1944-quebec-d178:
What passed between Roosevelt and Churchill at lunch on September 13, 1944, is known only at second hand. The editors draw on a memorandum by Harry White, the Treasury official, recording what Roosevelt told Morgenthau later that day. Churchill had been very glum during the conversation, according to this account.

Roosevelt said he had asked Churchill how he would like to have the steel business of Europe for twenty or thirty years. Churchill, he reported, seemed much excited over the possibility. The note also records a suggestion made at one of the day's meetings: that Fiorello La Guardia go to Italy as the president's representative and attend meetings of the Allied Control Commission.
frus-1944-quebec-d278: A one-sentence British memorandum, C.C.S. 682 of September 15, 1944, asks the American chiefs to take note of a single fact: Operation Highball would be available in the Eastern Theatre at the end of November 1944. frus-1944-quebec-d78: The editorial note listed as Document 78 was drafted by State Department historians. It sits inside the Quebec 1944 volume of conference papers. Editorial notes explain what the documents leave unsaid. They give background and point readers to related records in the series. Behind the note stands the September 1944 Quebec meeting. Roosevelt hosted Churchill there as Allied armies entered Germany. The note guides readers through the preparations for that summit.
frus-1945-50-intel-d178:
The meeting named in the title took place on 26 November 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 178, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The first peace-time setup paired the National Intelligence Authority at the top with the Central Intelligence Group below it.

The record runs item by item, the way the meeting itself ran, with each topic closed by the group's choice on it. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d278:
On 24 May 1948, Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter sent a memorandum to the National Security Council. Readers meet it as document 278 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The CIA had its law and its first chiefs; what it still lacked was a settled sense of its own limits.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. A reader can watch the system think on paper: a fact here, a doubt there, a choice asked for at the end. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d378:
A memorandum from the Under Secretary of State (Webb) reached the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) on 4 April 1949. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 378 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. With the Dulles Report now public inside the government, agencies were sorting out what to change and what to defend.

The memo form let a staff officer speak straight to a chief: here is the point, here are the facts, here is what is asked. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d78:
McCormack wrote to William Benton, assistant secretary for public and cultural relations, on 23 October 1945. Both men ran newish empires inside the State Department, Benton's being information and culture. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Where intelligence ends and public information begins was a live border question in 1945, since wartime agencies had mixed spying, analysis, and propaganda. McCormack writing to Benton shows the two office heads sorting that border between them. Readers get a look at a forgotten seam of the postwar build. The men who told America's story abroad had to share a department with the men who read the world's secrets. Neither side could swallow the other.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d178:
A way out of the Yugoslav deadlock appeared on 27 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew's top secret report to the Secretary of State, traveling with the President's party, carries the news in excerpt. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

Subasic has accepted King Peter's latest proposal. The exile government will resign and be formed again at once under Subasic, on a wider basis. The new government will then put the Tito–Subasic agreement into force, taking account of the King's two objections. If the counter-proposal fails, the King will agree to the regency clause instead. Tito has consented to Subasic's coming to Belgrade to carry the agreement out, the appointment of a regency among the steps. Subasic plans to leave on 29 January.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d278:
Prisoners of war head the matters Winant put to Stettinius on 28 January 1945. His letter from London, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, was written on the eve of the conference. The Russians, he explains, feel deeply about this problem, and the letter shows why.

Hundreds of thousands of Soviet people, brutally treated by the Germans, are being freed in growing numbers by the allied armies. Moscow is pressing London and Washington, through the military missions, for two-way agreements. Each government would treat the other's freed nationals by the standard it applies to its own soldiers. Civilians count the same as soldiers in the Russian view. Winant adds a confession of difficulty. The European Advisory Commission never got to grips with the question. Its special subcommittee never met, for want of instructions to him.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d378: Get this referred to the foreign ministers before there is trouble. That is the whole of Harry Hopkins's advice to the President in this note of February 7, 1945, passed during the fourth plenary meeting. The slip is one sentence long, signed with Hopkins's first name. Its link to that session rests on internal evidence and on a later account the editors cite. Small as it is, the note shows the adviser steering a heated debate toward the ministers' table, where bargains could be drafted in cooler language.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d478:
What Polish democrats wanted is summed up in this cable from Grew of February 6, 1945. The summary covers a memorandum by former Premier Mikolajczyk. The Polish people at home, it said, desired to regulate Polish-Soviet relations. They feared Poland would be forced into communism. Their hopes of independence rested on Britain and the United States.

The memorandum urged a guarantee by all three great powers. Frontier changes should embrace all frontiers at once. The eastern frontier should be settled by compromise, not unilateral dictation, and should favor Poland more than the Curzon Line did. Restitution should include Danzig and East Prussia. Grew's summary reached Yalta as the leaders drew the map the memorandum dreaded.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d78:
Two open items had to be settled before a United Nations conference could even be called. Acting Secretary Stettinius told the President so on 15 November 1944, in a memorandum printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The items were Security Council voting and invitations with initial membership.

Stettinius then lists the ways to reach agreement. The most promising, he writes, is a meeting of the three heads of government. Failing that, the three foreign ministers might meet, preferably in London. A third option sends the Under Secretary to London. The paper is a direct step toward the Big Three meeting that became Yalta.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d178:
General Eisenhower suggested putting the Danube question on the summit agenda in a message dated July 3, 1945. Only a paraphrased extract is printed, as document 178 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The full text appears in the second volume, as an enclosure to another document.

The surviving lines discuss an international problem: the internationalization of the Danube river. They say its urgency would suggest adding it to the agenda of the coming Big Three conference, if that action is thought proper. Control of the Danube, Europe's great east-west waterway, was contested ground. The Soviet Union dominated its lower course, while the Western powers wanted the river opened to free navigation. Even this fragment shows a field commander feeding a policy question up to the summit.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d278:
A briefing paper described the pending Austrian occupation zones in a paper dated June 23, 1945. The paper is document 278 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It covers the agreements the European Advisory Commission was finishing in London for Austria's zones of occupation and control machinery.

The zones are largely settled. Salzburg and Upper Austria south of the Danube go to the United States. Burgenland and Lower Austria go to the Soviets. Styria and Carinthia go to the British. The Tirol and Vorarlberg go to the French. The one main obstacle is the zoning of Vienna itself. After a recent reconnaissance mission, most differences look solvable except the airfields. Washington, London, and Paris each press for a field of their own near the capital. Moscow has so far offered only one field for all three. Talks to settle the point were under way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d378:
Notes on reparation, drafted at Babelsberg on July 14, 1945, try to fix the scope of the term before any division among claimants. Agreement, the paper argues, should first be sought on how reparation relates to other forms of compensation by Germany. Only then should the allies argue over shares.

War booty, it says, should be defined narrowly, ideally as only the equipment and supplies of the German armed forces. The net value of labor services by Germans outside Germany should be credited to the reparations account. Restitution should count both property Germany destroyed and property it carried off. The paper was used the next day with the British.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d478:
Allied Force Headquarters is defended in Kirk's top secret cable from Caserta of July 7, 1945. His mission had made clear, he writes, how essential it held the retention of allied troops in Europe, and American troops in particular, to the preservation of order. He need not stress its concurrence in the supreme commander's views along those lines.

So long as an allied military commitment lasts in the area, Kirk argues, the headquarters should preserve an allied character. It should be reduced in size and moved to Trieste, the vital strategic point in southeastern Europe. He also proposes abolishing the political adviser's office, its useful work passing to a liaison officer attached to the Rome embassy.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d578:
Moscow ambassador Averell Harriman reported again to the President and Secretary of State on July 13, 1945. His top secret wire is document 578 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It details the last, best offer China's T. V. Soong put to Stalin and Molotov.

Soong proposed joint railways with an equal board and a Chinese chairman. The Chinese Eastern line would have a Russian manager, the South Manchurian line a Chinese one. Dairen would stay a free port under Chinese rule, with docks leased to the Soviets for trade. Port Arthur would be a naval base under Soviet control for joint use. Stalin called the plan unsatisfactory and gave nothing back. Soong left for Chungking to consult Chiang, hoping Truman might win a compromise at Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d678:
An extract from James Dunn's Potsdam memo of July 14, 1945, covers Tangier. It is document 678 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers, drawn from his talk with Sir Alexander Cadogan. Dunn reported the item to Secretary Byrnes among many agenda points.

Cadogan reported that the Paris talks on Tangier had been suspended. His government had not yet answered the Russian request to join them. It felt it could not refuse, since the United States had already joined the talks. Dunn replied that he saw no basis for keeping Russia out. Cadogan then suggested a wider table if Russia came in. All the interested powers should be invited, the Belgians, Dutch, and Swedes among them. The Spaniards, he added, presumably would not be.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d78:
Ambassador Harriman appealed to Soviet official Andrei Vyshinsky in a letter dated June 19, 1945. The letter is document 78 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Eisenhower needed his advance party in Berlin the next day. They had to prepare housing, food, and communications for the American delegation. But the Soviet General Staff wanted to wait for Zhukov's return on June 28.

Harriman sets out the request in detail: General Parks, 50 officers, 175 enlisted men, and 50 trucks. He also asks free use of the Dessau-Berlin highway and the Halle-Berlin air route. A little over two weeks after June 28, he argues, would not leave enough time to get ready. He asks for approval that night so the movement can start in the morning.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1078:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk sent this extract of a telegram from Caserta on July 24, 1945. It reports a sharp exchange in Belgrade between the British ambassador and Marshal Tito. The ambassador had been ordered to protest Yugoslav radio and press propaganda, and fiery statements by Yugoslav leaders, on the Greek frontier and Venezia Giulia questions.

Tito answered that his own speeches only keep his people informed. Yugoslav propaganda on Greece, he said, replies to Greek attacks, and British newspapers share blame for the Venezia Giulia row. He rejected the argument, but agreed to seek direct talks with Athens to settle difficulties. The ambassador doubted the Yugoslav press would change its line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1178:
In a less common direction, the Acting Secretary of State wrote to the Secretary of State himself on 31 July 1945. Joseph Grew ran the department from Washington while Secretary Byrnes was at Potsdam. His message reported home-front business up to his chief at the talks.

The flow of cables usually ran from the summit to the capital. This one runs the other way: the home office briefing the team abroad. It shows the department's two halves keeping each other posted in the last days. A reader gets the whole circuit in one note, Washington speaking and Potsdam listening.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1278:
President Truman wrote to Generalissimo Stalin on 21 July 1945. Leader-to-leader notes were the summit's most direct channel. This one went from the American president to the Soviet chief in the middle of the talks' first week.

Such a message carried the sender's personal weight. It could soften a session, press a claim, or test the other man's mood between meetings. This note belongs to the pair of Truman-Stalin exchanges in the volume. Read with Stalin's reply of the following week, it shows the top of the alliance at work in its own words.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1378:
Charles Yost, executive secretary of the conference's central secretariat, wrote a memorandum on 9 August 1945, a week after Potsdam ended. The secretariat kept the summit's records, lists, and drafts in order. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Papers written after a conference closes often explain how its texts were made and filed. Yost's post at the secretariat put him at the center of that housekeeping. His memorandum helps readers trust the record itself, since it comes from the man charged with keeping it. It is a fitting late entry in the volume: the staff view of how a great meeting was wound up and its papers put away.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-78:
A dozen shipping topics fill the subject list of another unrecorded Potsdam conversation. Its editorial note is the seventy-eighth unnumbered item following document 710 in volume two. Troop shipping for the Pacific war dominates the list.

British vessels in the Pacific for Operation Coronet head the list. The United States agreed not to request conversion of eighteen British cargo vessels to troopships. That concession was tied to the allocation of the liner Milwaukee to the United States. Whether the Milwaukee would be converted in America or Britain, and crewed by which nation, was also debated. Britain's inability to supply France with coal that winter comes up, with U.S. shipping and coal support in view. Italian charter payments, Italian membership in the Maritime Authority, and the disposition of captured German vessels close a very full agenda.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d778:
A second Kirk report from Rome bears the date July 20, 1945, as document 778. Two dispatches in one day mark a full in-tray at the embassy. The ambassador in Italy kept Washington current as Potsdam began. This report joined the second Potsdam volume beside the first.

Paired same-day reports let readers split a post's business by theme. One may carry politics, the other a pressing case. Kirk's pair shows an embassy working several lines at once. The documents together give Rome's week a fuller shape. They show how much of diplomacy is simply keeping many threads from tangling.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d878:
Written for Assistant Secretary of State William Clayton on July 23, 1945, this working paper lays out advice on German economic matters at Potsdam. Its author is not named. The paper assumes the three powers will accept the supply policy set out in a memorandum on Poland's western boundary.

The advice would wind up the Reparations Commission and hand reparations to the zone commanders. Only broad deals struck in the Control Council would bind them. It also urges deleting Principle 18 and rewriting a clause on foreign credits to Germany. Two small edits would add currency, banking, and customs to the list of shared policy fields.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d978:
William Clayton cabled the Secretary of State from London on August 14, 1945, about captured German gold. At Potsdam, the Soviets gave up any claim to gold taken by Allied troops in Germany. Clayton stresses the reach of those words. Allied includes Soviet forces, and Germany includes the Soviet zone.

No big power, he adds, gave up its voice in deciding the gold's fate. Clayton backs the Gold Pot theory, pooling the gold for shared settlement. He advises handling its disposal with the general restitution problem, first through Pauley and the Reparations Commission. Failing agreement there, Generals Eisenhower and Clay would act in the Control Council.
frus-1969-76v10-d278: A 1969-1976 FRUS editorial note from the late Vietnam volume. The fall of Saigon neared. This note provides that context. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
gao-gaoreports-b-297078: Lifecare Management Partners doubled its November 2005 protest — two case numbers, one health-services fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firms challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-297378: Meggitt Safety Systems doubled its January 2006 protest — two case numbers, one safety-gear fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298478: An unnamed matter got its October 2006 GAO ruling, and the decision resolves the case on the record. The call applies the bid law to the facts. The ruling shows even the docket's mysteries get answers. The matter got its verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299978: A 2007 GAO ruling on three linked contract fights from AlliedBarton Security Services LLC. The guard giant challenged a trio of federal awards; the ruling works the claims one by one. The call shows GAO juggling repeat filings from a heavyweight of the hired-guard trade — and keeping each bid on its own merits.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-278: Defense chip labs got a GAO census in 2005, and the report covers the DOD-funded facilities doing research prototyping or production. The review counts the clean rooms. The microchips deserved the map. The facilities were listed. The microchips deserved the map.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-378: D.C.'s parklands got a GAO inventory in 2005, and the report covers the National Park Service's managed properties in the capital. The review lists the grounds. The monuments' lawns were counted. The properties were cataloged. The monuments' lawns were counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-478: Voter registration lists needed better data in 2005, and GAO's report says additional figures could help officials maintain accurate rolls. The findings demand the information. The report warns that the voters deserved clean lists. The data had to come. The voters deserved clean lists.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-878: Federal tax system costs got a GAO summary in 2005, and the report compiles estimates of the compliance burden. The findings do the math. The report shows the paperwork mountain was measured. The estimates had to be summarized. The paperwork mountain was measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-378: The FAA got a congressional oversight case study in 2006, and GAO's report shows how performance and budget information could enhance supervision. The findings make the case. The report warns that the skies' agency deserved watching. The oversight had to be informed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-678: Corporate do-overs kept coming in 2006, and GAO's report updates the trends, market impacts, and enforcement around financial restatements. The findings count the corrections. The report warns that the restated books told a cautionary tale. The trends had to be watched.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-978: Blood diamonds needed tighter policing in 2006, and GAO's report says agency action was required to enforce the clean diamond trade law. The findings demand the enforcement. The report warns that the gems should not fund wars. The trade had to be clean.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1078: Flood insurance money was leaking to middlemen in 2007 — GAO's report says FEMA's watch over payments to private insurers needed muscle. The findings question whether the firms selling federal flood policies earned their cut. In a program already drowning in red ink, every wasted dollar stung twice.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-278: The visitor-tracking program's budget needed justifying in 2007, and GAO's report says the planned spending had to be adequately defined. The findings demand the details. The report warns that the border's digital eye should not be bought blind. The dollars had to match the mission.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-478: Wetland permits bought with outside cash drew GAO's eye in 2007 — the report says the Corps needed to keep those decisions clean. The findings probe the funding influence. The report's principle: a permit is a public trust, not a purchased favor.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-578: The Pentagon's spy eyes needed joining up in 2007 — GAO's report says its intelligence and surveillance systems could share more and waste less. The findings target the stovepipes. The report's vision: one picture from many sensors, not many pictures from one war.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-678: The money cops were grading themselves in 2007 — GAO's report says the financial regulators had adopted key performance habits, with room to grow further. The findings measure the measurers against best practice. The report's gentle prod: even regulators need report cards of their own.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-78: Afghanistan's poppy fields were winning in 2007, and GAO's report says despite better efforts, worsening security threatened the drug-control goals. The findings document the losing battle. The report warns that the bullets were beating the eradication. The war on drugs was losing to the war.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-1078: GAO published its findings on next Generation Air Transportation System: Status of Systems Acquisition and the Transition to the Next Generation Air Transportation System in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-678: The Government Accountability Office dug into young Adults With Serious Mental Illness: Some States and Federal Agencies Are Taking Steps to Address Their Transition Challenges in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
geber-works-russell-1678:
Richard Russell gave The Works of Geber English dress in 1678. Geber was the Latin name for tracts tied to Jabir ibn Hayyan. The core work is the Summa Perfectionis, the Sum of Perfection. It is a root text of the alchemy of the West.

Clear rules tell how to test, purge, and join the base stuffs of the art. Geber gives the first clear tale of strong acids and their use. He sorts metals by their make and tells how each may be raised. The book set the lab craft of alchemy on a firm base.
hardy-return-native-1878:
Thomas Hardy published The Return of the Native in 1878, setting it on the wild Egdon Heath in his fictional Wessex. Hardy knew this Dorset landscape from childhood. The heath itself broods over the story almost like a character.

Clym Yeobright, the native, returns from Paris hoping to teach the local people. He marries the restless Eustacia Vye, who dreams only of escaping the heath for a glamorous life. Their mismatch pulls in a former lover, a reddleman, and Clym's stern mother. Misread letters and chance meetings steer everyone toward tragedy. The novel is one of Hardy's most admired studies of longing and fate.
haug-essays-sacred-language-parsis-1878:
Martin Haug's Essays on the Sacred Language, Writings, and Religion of the Parsis appeared at London in 1878. The second edition was edited and enlarged by E. W. West. Haug, a German scholar who worked in India, founded the Western study of the Avesta, the Zoroastrian scriptures. His essays sort the Gathas, the oldest hymns ascribed to Zoroaster himself, from later layers of the texts.

An outline of a Pahlavi-Pazand glossary closes the volume, a tool for students of Middle Persian. Haug's work established Pahlavi studies and put Parsi religion on a scholarly footing in Europe. The book became the most cited nineteenth-century work on its subject. West's enlargement kept it current after Haug's early death. It still introduces the field's history.
james-daisy-miller-1878:
Henry James published Daisy Miller in 1878, first in an English magazine after American editors balked. James was then an expatriate writer shuttling between America and Europe. The novella made his name on both sides of the Atlantic and defined his great theme: the American abroad.

Daisy Miller, a pretty, free-spirited girl from Schenectady, tours Switzerland and Rome with no sense of European rules. The young American Winterbourne watches her, torn between attraction and the colony's snobbish verdict. Her friendship with an Italian escort ruins her name, and a Roman fever ends the story. James never quite says whether Daisy was innocent or foolish. Readers have argued it for a century.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micha-10778:
