Micha is one of the briefest entries in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, just two numbered lines by Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn. It exists to sort out a minor biblical name. Readers who land on it are pointed to the fuller article on Micah for the family line it belongs to.

The first figure is a son of Mephibosheth, listed here with a cross-reference to the third Micah of the main entry rather than a story of his own. The second is one of the Levites who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah, cited to chapter ten of Nehemiah, verse eleven. Nothing more is claimed for either man, and the entry's honesty about that is its whole value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morais-sabato-1:
Sabato Morais, an American rabbi born at Leghorn on April 13, 1823, is given a full early life by Cyrus Adler and Cyrus L. Sulzberger in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The family had fled Portugal's Inquisition generations before. His father Samuel was an ardent republican, at one time imprisoned for his political views, in an Italy struggling for freedom.

Responsibility came early: as a child Sabato earned money teaching Hebrew hymns and prayers to other children, while studying under Rabbi Piperno and winning honorable mention in belles-lettres. He commanded Aramaic, French, and Spanish beside Hebrew and Italian. In 1845 he went to London to apply for the vacant post of assistant ḥazzan of the Spanish and Portuguese congregation — the first step toward Philadelphia, where he died in 1897.
john-cross-ascent-mount-carmel-1578:
John of the Cross wrote the Ascent of Mount Carmel in Spain in the late 1500s. David Lewis turned the work into English. John was a Carmelite monk and a close friend of Teresa of Avila. His book is a strict guide to prayer and the dark night.

A poem of the soul's climb frames the whole text. John glosses each line to teach how to drop all ties to sense and self. The dark night, he says, strips the soul bare for union with God. The book stands with his Dark Night as a peak of Spain's soul lore.
jonston-description-four-footed-beasts-1:
John Jonston, a Polish-born scholar who worked in the Dutch world of learning, wrote vast Latin surveys of nature. This English Description of the Nature of Four-footed Beasts appeared in 1678. It brought the great Central European natural history to English readers in their own tongue.

Jonston gathers beasts both real and rumored, from the lion to the manticore. Each entry packs in names, habits, and reports drawn from many authors. His learning is deep and his pages are crowded. English readers could set this book beside Topsell's earlier beast book and compare them. Together the two show how Europe pictured animals before modern science.
lessing-dramatic-works-bell-1878:
Ernest Bell's Dramatic Works of Lessing, published in 1878, holds four plays that remade German drama. Miss Sara Sampson brought everyday middle-class sorrow to the stage in place of kings. Philotas gives a captured young prince one fierce choice about honor and death.

Emilia Galotti, the darkest of the four, shows a prince's lust destroying a virtuous girl and her family. Nathan the Wise closes the volume with its plea for tolerance among faiths. Bell's Nathan differs from Taylor's older version, and the two are kept as distinct translations. Together the four plays show why Lessing is counted the founder of modern German drama. No other single volume shows his range so well.
mackey-encyclopedia-freemasonry-1878:
Albert G. Mackey was the great voice of Masonic lore in the States. His Encyclopedia of Freemasonry came out in 1878. Its full title adds the kindred sciences to the craft. The book aims to hold all a Mason might need to know in one tome.

Heads run from rites and signs to lives of famed Masons of the past. Long tales give the craft's past, its laws, and the sense of its marks. Mackey writes with care and with love for the lore. The book stayed the stock desk guide for the craft for scores of years.
maxwell-ether-1878:
James Clerk Maxwell wrote this piece on the ether for the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1878. The ether was the unseen stuff men thought filled all space. Light waves, they held, must wave in something, and the ether was that something.

Maxwell sums up what the ether must be like to bear light at such speed. He tells how stiff and yet how free of drag it must be, from the proof at hand. Short and calm, the piece is the great man's own word on what the ether was meant to be.
musaeum-hermeticum-reformatum-et-amplifi: Musaeum hermeticum, reformatum et amplificatum, 1678. The hermetic museum. This book preserves that collection. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
openalex-w1990847378: Science moves fast — rapid communications keep pace with discovery. This 2012 work titled 'Rapid communications' presents brief, timely scientific reports. The thin catalog record hides the details, but the format serves fast-moving findings that can't wait.
openalex-w2019284478: The deep sea is Earth's largest ecosystem — and no longer untouched. A 2011 review surveyed human impact on the deep sea: fisheries, oil and gas, and the new tech reaching the last great wilderness. The paper warned the frontier is closing.
openalex-w2052410578: Vivax malaria is harder to eliminate — its genes explain why. A 2015 study found Plasmodium vivax populations more diverse and less structured than local falciparum populations. The comparison explained vivax's stubborn staying power in the field.
openalex-w2070050178: Gene lists need meaning — Enrichr finds it. A 2013 paper introduces Enrichr, a web tool for gene-list enrichment analysis. The platform turned raw gene lists into biological insight fast — for any biologist with data in hand.
openalex-w2115083578: Metabolic syndrome stalks Latin America's cities. A 2009 CARMELA study measured metabolic syndrome prevalence in Latin America and its link to early artery disease. The one-time study covered 7 urban centers — heart risk, mapped for the region.
openalex-w2136197678: HER2 drugs worked in gastric cancer — ToGA proved it. A 2014 ToGA report covered HER2 tests in gastric cancer. The drug plus chemo added 2.7 months median survival for HER2+ patients — a win for targeted therapy.
openalex-w2155678178: A 2014 Physical Review Letters paper reports measurements from BICEP2, a telescope at the South Pole built to hunt for inflationary gravitational waves. The instrument scanned the cosmic microwave background — the faint afterglow of the Big Bang — for a swirling pattern called B-mode polarization in degree-sized patches of sky. The team presents the signal it found, a search for direct evidence of how the universe expanded in its first moments.
openalex-w2211460678: At the Large Hadron Collider, each interesting collision arrives buried under dozens of simultaneous ones — "pile-up" that smears the debris physicists want to study. This 2016 paper describes the techniques ATLAS developed during Run 1 to clean up jets, the sprays of particles from high-energy quarks. The methods separate the real collision from the noise, keeping measurements sharp as the collider's intensity climbs.
openalex-w2996050378: This 2019 study uses genomic-scale data to reconstruct the phylogenetic systematics and evolution of the spider infraorder Mygalomorphae — tarantulas, trapdoor spiders, and their kin, one of spiders' three great lineages. The genomic tree clarifies relationships among these ancient, burrowing spiders.
openalex-w4412745578: Python powers modern labs, and this paper shows how one lab uses it. The authors shared real examples: crunching data and automating boring tasks in Python. They pitched its ease for scientists. A friendly how-to paper straight from the lab bench.
openalex-w7204994078: After colon surgery, how the bowel is tucked back may matter. This trial of 160 patients tested whether small-intestine arrangement affects gut function after laparoscopic colectomy. The team compared the new layout against standard care. A surgical study of plumbing details with real consequences.
plos-pbio-0020078:
Habibeh Khoshbouei, Namita Sen, Bipasha Guptaroy, and others studied the dopamine transporter in PLOS Biology in 2004. This protein normally clears dopamine, a key brain signal, from the gap between nerve cells. Amphetamine flips its action and pushes dopamine out instead.

The team found that a phosphate tag on the transporter's front end is needed for that flip. Without the tag, amphetamine cannot trigger the outflow. The detail matters for understanding how stimulant drugs work at the molecular level. It also marks a possible control point. A drug that guards that tag might blunt amphetamine's effects while leaving normal dopamine clearing intact.
plos-pbio-0020178:
Daniella Bianchi-Frias, Amir Orian, Jeffrey J. Gross, and their team mapped a gene switch in the fruit fly for PLOS Biology in 2004. The switch is a protein called Hairy, which turns target genes off during embryo growth. The authors found which genes Hairy binds and which helper proteins it recruits.

A switch is only as good as the helpers it brings to each site. By listing targets and helpers together, the study shows how one protein can fine-tune many genes in different ways. That matters because Hairy-like switches shape body plans in many animals. The fly data gives a concrete parts list for a whole class of gene control.
plos-pone-0000078:
Marco Marani, Tommaso Zillio, Enrica Belluco, and their team modeled plant growth patterns in PLOS ONE in 2006. In marshes and other wetlands, plants form stripes and patches that long puzzled observers. Older models treated the pattern as a neutral result of random spread. The authors show that view falls short.

Their work argues the patterns are non-neutral: feedback between plants and water flow shapes them. Plants slow the water, trap soil, and change their own living conditions, which then drives the stripes. Getting the cause right matters for restoring wetlands, since planting by the wrong model wastes effort. The paper is a case for active feedback in ecology.
plos-pone-0000178:
Hany A. El-Shemy, Ahmed M. Aboul-Enein, Khalid Mostafa Aboul-Enein, and colleagues published this pharmacology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It reports that extracts from willow leaves contain agents that act against tumors. The extracts were tested against three cell types and showed anti-tumor effects.

Willow already gave medicine aspirin, so its leaves are a plausible place to look for active compounds. The authors screen the extracts and report the killing effect on the tested cells. Work at this stage is an early filter: it cannot prove a drug, but it flags plant chemistry worth isolating and testing further.
plos-pone-0000278:
Colleen V. Chien published this health policy paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It compares brand-name and generic supply of HIV/AIDS drugs for sub-Saharan Africa, where the epidemic hit hardest and drug access was a global controversy. The author asks how the two supply routes stack up in getting medicines to patients.

Price was only part of the access problem; supply chains, patents, and donations all played roles. The paper compares the brand and generic channels directly. It contributed evidence to the debate over how poor countries should source life-saving drugs, a question that shaped global health policy.
plos-pone-0000378:
Kun-Lin Zhang and colleagues built a model of a human defense protein, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The protein, APOBEC3G, is part of the body's built-in defense against viruses such as HIV, which fights back with a protein of its own. Knowing the defender's three-dimensional shape is key to understanding that struggle.

Since a full experimental structure was not in hand, the team modeled the protein's structure from related knowledge. A model like this gives researchers a working picture. It shows which parts of the protein do the antiviral work. It also shows where a virus might attack it. Such models often guide lab experiments and, later, drug design.
plos-pone-0000478:
Marcin R. Przewloka and colleagues took apart the kinetochore of the fruit fly piece by piece, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The kinetochore is the protein machine that grips chromosomes and hauls them apart during cell division. Their molecular analysis covered the composition and assembly of its core in Drosophila melanogaster.

Knowing which proteins form the core, and in what order they assemble, is basic to understanding how division stays accurate. Errors here leave cells with missing or extra chromosomes. Fly kinetochores offer a simpler model of the same machine that operates in human cells, where its failure is tied to cancer and birth defects.
plos-pone-0000578:
Marina Pfalz, Heiko Vogel, and Thomas Mitchell-Olds mapped cabbage-family resistance to a specialist caterpillar, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Pieris brassicae, the large white butterfly, feeds on crucifers like cabbage and Arabidopsis. The team mapped QTL, genome regions affecting a trait, for resistance against this herbivore in a new Arabidopsis inbred line population, Da(1)-12×Ei-2.

Resistance QTL point to the genes a plant uses to fend off its specialist enemy, which has evolved countermeasures of its own. Such maps guide both evolutionary studies of plant defense and breeding of tougher crops. A new mapping population gives the community fresh genetic material to work with.
plos-pone-0000678:
James Ronald and Joshua M. Akey traced how gene expression differences evolve in yeast, writing for PLOS ONE in 2007. Their subject was expression QTLs, genome spots linked to how strongly a gene is expressed, in Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the common baker's yeast. The forces shaping expression variation promise insight into how evolution works at the molecular level.

Most studies of expression evolution had taken other routes, comparing species or surveying variation. Tracking the QTLs themselves shows where in the genome change accumulates. Yeast offers huge populations and full genomes, making it a clean test case. The results feed the broader question of how visible diversity arises from gene regulation.
plos-pone-0000778:
Jesse L. Clark, Carlos F. Caceres, Andres G. Lescano and colleagues surveyed sexual behavior among low-income urban men in Peru, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Peru has a concentrated HIV epidemic in which men who have sex with men are most at risk. The team reports the lifetime prevalence of same-sex sexual contact in the general male population, regardless of sexual identity, along with linked risk behaviors.

Identity and behavior do not always match, and prevention built on identity alone misses people. A probability-based survey of the general population catches behavior that targeted studies overlook. Numbers like these shape where HIV programs in Peru should aim their outreach, testing, and teaching.
plos-pone-0000878:
Alexandra Nunes, Joao Gomes, Sally Mead and colleagues compared a gene family across strains of Chlamydia trachomatis, in PLOS ONE in 2007. This germ lives inside host cells and is a leading cause of eye and genital disease worldwide. Its pmp gene family codes for nine membrane proteins whose roles are still being worked out.

The team profiled how strongly each pmp gene is used in lab reference strains versus strains taken from patients. Differences there may point to which proteins matter most during real infection. The work adds detail to a germ that is common, often silent and still hard to control.
plos-pone-0000978:
Federica Verra, Jacques Simpore, George Warimwe and colleagues studied how two hemoglobin variants affect immunity to malaria, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hemoglobin C and S are altered forms of the red blood cell protein, common where malaria is present. A proposed shield from hemoglobin C involves the parasite's own surface protein being shown abnormally on infected cells.

That odd display comes with weaker sticking of infected cells to vessel walls. The team examine the role of both variants in acquired immunity against Plasmodium falciparum malaria. The work links a genetic trait, kept common by malaria itself, to the immune side of protection.
plos-pone-0001078:
Tobias von der Haar optimized protein extraction for measuring yeast proteins in absolute amounts, in a solo PLOS ONE article from 2007. Counting the actual number of protein molecules in a cell is hard to do well. Newer approaches, from systems biology to metabolic control analysis, need exactly those numbers.

Existing extraction protocols lose or distort part of the protein pool. Von der Haar presents a refined method for counting yeast proteins. If proteins are lost unevenly, every downstream number is skewed. A better extraction is unglamorous groundwork, but absolute claims about cell contents stand or fall on it. The paper serves labs moving from relative to absolute measures.
plos-pone-0001178:
The fruit fly's nervous system is built by cells that must choose neural fates at the right places. Savita Ayyar, Daniela Pistillo, and Manuel Calleja describe two roles for the fly versions of NF-kappaB proteins. Their account appeared in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The three proteins are Dorsal, Dif, and Relish.

First, these factors regulate a gene called scute as sensory organ precursors are singled out from clusters of cells. The authors also describe a second, distinct role in peripheral nervous system development. NF-kappaB is better known for immune defense, so its developmental jobs in the fly widen the family's known territory.
plos-pone-0001278:
Malaria vaccines have a long record of failure, so new delivery platforms are watched closely. Shinji Okitsu and colleagues report a phase 1a clinical trial of a virosomal malaria peptide vaccine, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Virosomes are hollow influenza virus shells used to carry vaccine peptides on their surface.

Peptides given this way had induced solid antibody responses in animals, and high titers in volunteers before. The authors report a long-lasting sporozoite-inhibitory antibody response, antibodies that block the parasite stage injected by mosquitoes. Early-phase results like these decide whether a vaccine concept moves on.
plos-pone-0001378:
Perry Ridge, Yan Zhang, and Vadim Gladyshev wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on copper in living things. Copper is a trace metal that all life forms need in small amounts. Cells use it in proteins that handle oxygen and energy. Too much copper is toxic, so cells must guard it with care.

The authors compared genes for copper carriers and copper using proteins across many species. From those maps they traced how copper use changed over time. They also probed how copper use links to oxygen in the world. The work gives a broad view of how one metal helped shape life as oxygen rose on Earth.
plos-pone-0001478:
Solen Kernéis and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE model of flu pandemic control. Plans to curb a pandemic are well studied in broad terms. Less studied is how the shape of spread, in place and time, changes which plan works best. The team used a model that tracks spread between linked towns with air travel.

They varied the pandemic's profile and tested control steps against each shape. Their work shows the best plan can hinge on that shape. A plan that wins for one spread pattern may lag for another. Health teams should thus plan for a range of shapes, not one fixed script.
plos-pone-0001578:
David Bell and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE trial report on malaria drug mixes in Malawi. An old drug had regained its power there after a newer mix took over first line care. A second drug had shown grave side effects when used for prevention. The team ran a blind trial of mixes built on the standard pair.

They compared how well each mix cured malaria, how safe each was, and how each shaped drug resistance. Malawi's shift in first line drugs is a rare natural test. Its lessons guide drug policy across Africa, where resistance can undo years of gains in a short span.
plos-pone-0001678:
Christian Leisner and co-authors presented a faster way to build a key immune test tool in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Killer T cells, or CTLs, recognize infected cells by the peptide-MHC complexes on their surface: small protein fragments displayed by MHC class I molecules. Tetramers, lab-made clusters of these complexes, let scientists find and count specific T cells.

Older tetramer production took many steps. The authors' one-pot, mix-and-read method assembles them in a single reaction. The full text gives the recipe, the quality checks, and the T-cell tests they ran. Simpler tetramers lower the cost of tracking immune responses in vaccine trials, infections, and cancer studies.
plos-pone-0001778:
Paul Wilmes, Margaret Wexler, and Philip L. Bond read the protein output of a wastewater treatment community in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Activated sludge systems clean sewage with a mixed microbial culture. One prized process is enhanced biological phosphorus removal, in which microbes pull phosphorus from wastewater so it does not pollute waterways.

Using metaproteomics, identifying highly expressed proteins from the whole mixed culture, the team found functional evidence of the microbial transformations behind phosphorus removal. The full text gives the reactor setup and the protein list. Matching proteins to processes shows which organisms do the work in the sludge, knowledge operators can use to keep treatment plants running well.
plos-pone-0001878:
Delphine Quelard and colleagues reported a hidden switch inside a common body protein in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Collagens, the tough fibers that hold tissues together, can carry tucked-away parts that steer cell growth or cell death once freed. One collagen, type eighteen, comes in three forms that differ at one end.

The team studied the third form and found that it holds a part much like Frizzled, a known signal catcher. They show that this part blocks the Wnt signal path, a key route that tells cells to grow and divide. A brake built into a fiber protein is a neat find, since that path drives many cancers when stuck on.
plos-pone-0001978:
Karin Weldingh and Peter Andersen tested a skin test that flags TB cases bound to worsen, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Treating people whose TB is still silent but advancing, before they can spread it, would break chains of transmission in hard-hit regions. The hard part is knowing whose silent case will progress.

The team gave guinea pigs infected with TB a skin test using two proteins from the bacterium, ESAT-6 and CFP10. As the title states, the test response predicted which animals went on to disease. A test that sorts silent cases by risk could aim preventive drugs where they help most.
plos-pone-0002078:
Charlotte Gustafsson and co-authors profiled the genes of immune cells at the womb's inner lining, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. In pregnancy, macrophages sit in the decidua, the lining where the placenta meets the womb. They are thought to play a key regulatory role at the maternal-fetal interface. Their global gene expression profile was not known.

Using a micro-array of about fourteen thousand genes, the team read the full pattern in first trimester decidual macrophages. As the title states, the evidence points to an immunosuppressive phenotype, cells set to calm rather than attack. That calm is what lets a fetus, half foreign to the mother, grow in peace.
plos-pone-0002178:
Brit Winnen and co-authors studied the order in which a gut bacterium injects its proteins into host cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Salmonella Typhimurium uses a needle-like system, the SPI-1 type III secretion system, to push effector proteins into the cells it infects. Those proteins then bend host cell signals toward disease.

The team focused on one effector, SipA, and showed that the injected proteins follow a ranking, a hierarchy of transport. Knowing the order matters, because the first proteins in may set the stage for the rest. The work maps one step in how Salmonella takes over a cell.
plos-pone-0002278:
Beatrice Oneda and co-authors mapped an enzyme in the rat kidney and its change in kidney disease, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Meprin is a metal-cutting enzyme found in the brush border membranes of kidney tubule cells, where urine is processed. Its presence elsewhere in the kidney was less clear.

The authors present the first report of the meprin beta form in rat glomerular epithelial cells, the cells that wrap the kidney's filters. They also found its expression differs in glomerulonephritis, an inflammation of those filters. The pattern suggests meprin beta plays a part in the disease of the filtering unit.
plos-pone-0002378:
Work from Walker and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Sarah Walker, Tim E. A. Peto, Lily O'Connor, and others. Its subject is are There Better Methods of Monitoring MRSA Control than Bacteraemia Surveillance? An Observational Database Study. Despite a substantial burden of non-bacteraemic methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) disease, most MRSA surveillance schemes are based on bacteraemias.

Using bacteraemia as an outcome, trends at hospital level are difficult to discern, due to random variation. Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002478:
In 2008, Tarasov and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits Kirill V. Tarasov, Yelena S. Tarasova, Wai Leong Tam, and others. Its subject is b-MYB Is Essential for Normal Cell Cycle Progression and Chromosomal Stability of Embryonic Stem Cells. The transcription factor B-Myb is present in all proliferating cells, and in mice engineered to remove this gene.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work.
plos-pone-0002578:
A research team led by Patel reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Alpa V. Patel, Iona Cheng, Federico Canzian, and others. Its subject is iGF-1 , IGFBP-1 , and IGFBP-3 Polymorphisms Predict Circulating IGF Levels but Not Breast Cancer Risk. The title goes on to note findings from the Breast and Prostate Cancer Cohort Consortium (BPC3). IGF-1 has been shown to promote proliferation of normal epithelial breast cells.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002678:
Charlotte K. Hemelrijk led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with female dominance over males in primates: Self-Organisation and sexual dimorphism. Authorship is credited in the record to Charlotte K. Hemelrijk and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. The processes that underlie the formation of the dominance hierarchy in a group are since long under debate. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002778:
Published in PLOS ONE in 2008, research by John P. A. Ioannidis and colleagues addresses measuring Co-Authorship and Networking-Adjusted scientific impact. The full author list in the catalog record begins with John P. A. Ioannidis, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Appraisal of the scientific impact of researchers, teams and institutions with productivity and citation metrics has major repercussions. The summary also notes a further point. Funding and promotion of individuals and survival of teams and institutions depend on publications and citations. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication. The full text can be read in the library, and this summary adds nothing beyond the record and abstract held for the entry.
plos-pone-0002878:
Matthew T. Bishop, Diane L. Ritchie, Robert G. Will and co-authors checked in 2008 whether the agent of variant Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease changes after spread by blood. Cases of vCJD passed on through transfusion had raised a sharp question. A changed agent might grow more virulent or adapt to new hosts.

Published in PLOS ONE, the study compares the strain after this second route of spread with the original form. Its title reports no major change in the agent strain. That finding matters for blood safety policy, since it speaks to what transfusion-linked cases mean for future risk.
plos-pone-0002978:
Pasqualino Loi, Kazutsugu Matsukawa, Grazyna Ptak and co-authors used freeze-dried cells for nuclear transfer in 2008. Simple organisms survive drying, and freeze-drying is the standard way to store bacteria and yeast long term. Applying it to mammalian cells for cloning was a newer attempt.

Their title reports that freeze-dried somatic cells can direct embryonic development after nuclear transfer. In plain terms, nuclei from dried cells still carried working developmental instructions. Published in PLOS ONE, the result suggests dried storage might one day preserve genetic material without deep freezing. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003078:
Caroline Conte, Elodie Riant, Céline Toutain and co-authors traced feedback loops between FGF2 and HIF-1 alpha in 2008. FGF2 is a major factor in angiogenesis and arteriogenesis, the growth of new vessels, yet control of its expression was poorly documented. Its RNA holds an internal entry site that lets translation start mid-message.

Under hypoxia, low oxygen, FGF2 is translationally induced and joins negative and positive feedback loops with HIF-1 alpha, the master low-oxygen factor. Published in PLOS ONE, the loops fine-tune vessel growth where oxygen runs short, as in tumors and wounds. Readers can follow the full methods and data in the complete text of the article.
plos-pone-0003178:
Heiko Müller and Francesco Mancuso present a tool for co-occurrence networks in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Co-occurrence analysis is often used in text mining, comparative genomics, and promoter analysis. The methods and statistical models used to judge whether linked items truly associate are quite diverse, however, and hard to compare.

They present NetCutter, with a general approach to identification and analysis of such networks. Readers get a shared method for a task that appears in many fields. A common tool can make results easier to check, repeat, and compare across studies that look unrelated at first glance.
plos-pone-0003278: Nicolas Schleinitz and colleagues published a PLOS ONE study in 2008 on natural killer cells, a type of immune cell. The title states its subject: how activation receptors are recruited, or drawn in, at immune synapses where these cells are being held back. No abstract beyond the title was supplied, so this record states no findings.
plos-pone-0003378:
Raúl Alelú-Paz and co-authors improved a staining method for brain tissue in this 2008 paper. Staining lets scientists see one chosen protein inside a slice of tissue. Fixing chemicals used to store human brains tend to hide those proteins. For thirty years, that masking effect had limited work on stored brain samples.

The team presents a new way to unmask the hidden proteins before staining. Their method brought back clear signals in human brain tissue. Stored brains are a key resource for studying diseases of the mind and nerves. A better unmasking step means old samples can answer new questions.
plos-pone-0003478:
Vijay Chickarmane and Carsten Peterson modeled early cell fate choices in this 2008 paper. Three factors, Oct4, Sox2, and Nanog, form a self-reinforcing network in stem cells. That network keeps embryonic stem cells able to renew and stay flexible. Rival signals between factors push cells toward fixed roles.

Their computational model follows that tug of war in time. It shows how cells settle as stem cells, trophectoderm, or endoderm. Trophectoderm and endoderm are two early embryo layers. The model captures the logic behind life's first branching choices. The same three factors are still core tools in stem cell labs today.
plos-pone-0003578:
Josef Wagner and co-authors searched gut biopsies from children with Crohn's disease in this 2008 paper. Reading bacterial 16S ribosomal genes can identify gut flora members. That method had already implicated some bacterial families in bowel inflammation. The team used ileal biopsies, from the last part of the small gut.

They identified and characterized Pseudomonas DNA in those samples. Finding this germ adds to the microbial census of Crohn's. Gut flora composition may shape inflammatory bowel disease in the young. Each named suspect narrows the hunt for triggers. Crohn's often starts in youth and lasts for life, with flares and calm spells.
plos-pone-0003678:
Alex Proekt, Jane Wong, Yuriy Zhurov, and colleagues published this theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008. An animal's nervous system does not act alone; it stays coupled to its surroundings at every moment. That coupling limits the dynamics both sides must have for adaptive behavior to arise.

Building on earlier computer work, the authors derive which dynamical properties the nervous system needs. From those properties, they show, suitable behavior in the environment can be predicted. The study reads smart behavior out of the shared physics of brain and world, rather than from the brain alone.
plos-pone-0003778:
Hugh R. Woodland and Andrew M. Fry published this evolution study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Centrioles are small barrels that organize cells and build cilia and flagella. Pix proteins are parts of vertebrate centrioles found in most eukaryotes. The authors made a wide survey across the tree of life.

They mapped where Pix proteins occur and how their forms vary between organisms. Alongside, they surveyed which organisms carry flagella, cilia, and centrioles, using published records. The census clarifies how these ancient structures arose and diversified across eukaryotes. The Pix family now has a map for deeper study.
plos-pone-0003878:
Christopher E. Bagwell, Swapna Bhat, Gary M. Hawkins, and co-authors sequenced a tough bacterium in 2008. Their PLOS ONE article reports the genome of Kineococcus radiotolerans SRS30216. The microbe came from a high-level radioactive waste site at Savannah River. It withstands gamma radiation at levels close to the famous Deinococcus radiodurans.

The U.S. Department of Energy Joint Genome Institute carried out the sequencing. Reading the full genome lets scientists hunt for genes behind the extreme resistance. Those genes could guide cleanup methods for nuclear waste sites. They may also suggest new uses in industry where radiation harms other microbes.
plos-pone-0003978:
Adrian Nestor, Jean M. Vettel, and Michael J. Tarr studied how face tasks shape brain coding in 2008. Faces are sorted in many ways, which strains recognition systems. Two basic tasks are spotting a face and telling which face it is. The authors asked whether those tasks need different codes.

Their PLOS ONE article explores how task demands reshape feature use. Detection may lean on broad cues, while individuation needs fine detail. Neural patterns shifted with the task a person was doing. The work shows face reading is flexible, not one fixed process. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004078:
Hui Wang and Dimitrios Vavylonis modeled actin cable building in fission yeast in a 2008 PLOS ONE article. The formin protein For3p starts actin cables at yeast cell tips. Those cables guide growth toward the cell ends. Prior experiments hinted at how assembly might proceed.

Their model tests whether For3p behavior can explain cable growth. It joins For3p placement, actin polymerization, and cable movement in one scheme. A working model predicts what new experiments should measure. It shows how simple protein rules yield ordered cell structures. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004178:
Yungok Ihm and colleagues published this structural study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rev is a regulatory protein that equine infectious anemia virus, a relative of HIV, cannot do without. It grabs viral RNA messages that are not fully spliced. It then escorts them out of the nucleus. That step is required before the virus can build its structural proteins.

No full picture of this protein's shape existed. The team built a structural model of Rev from the horse virus. A model of how Rev is folded helps scientists compare it with the HIV version and understand how this viral switch works.
plos-pone-0004278:
Olivier Béaslas and colleagues published this gut study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The intestine absorbs dietary lipids and delivers them to the body as triglyceride-rich lipoproteins. How enterocytes, the intestine's absorptive cells, regulate that process matters, because long post-meal spikes in blood lipids are harmful.

The team describe a new role for SR-BI, also called CLA-1, a receptor best known from cholesterol handling. They present it as a sensor of dietary lipids in enterocytes. A gut sensor that tastes incoming fat could be a target for controlling blood lipids after meals.
plos-pone-0004378:
Public health teams watch for disease outbreaks as early as they can. One newer signal is what sick people type into medical web sites. Anette Hulth, Gustaf Rydevik, and Annika Linde tested that signal in Sweden. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper used flu as the test case. They studied queries sent to a medical web site.

The authors asked whether flu-related searches rise and fall with real flu spread. Search data arrives fast and costs little to collect. If queries track illness well, they can support older reporting systems. The paper is an early test of web data for outbreak watching. It helped pave the way for later digital disease tracking work.
plos-pone-0004478:
A gene switch called Sp3 plays two opposing roles in tumors, report Khadija Essafi-Benkhadir, Sebastien Grosso, Alexandre Puissant, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sp3 is a transcription factor, a protein that turns genes on or off. It has been described as both a blocker and a booster of gene activity, so its role in cancer was unclear.

The team studied why Sp3 builds up in aggressive tumors. They report that it can act as an inducer of apoptosis, the program that makes cells die on order. Yet its presence also marks the most aggressive tumors. Holding both facts at once is the point: a protein that can kill cancer cells may still signal danger when a tumor learns to live with it.
plos-pone-0004578:
A new statistical measure for gene-environment interaction is proposed by Xuesen Wu, Li Jin, and Momiao Xiong in PLOS ONE in 2009. Interest in how genes and environment interact is high, since most diseases arise from both. Yet the essential issue of how to define and detect such interactions remains unresolved, as the authors note.

They define interaction as a stochastic dependence, a statistical link between gene and environment in shaping a trait. They then use mutual information, a measure from information theory, to test for it. A clear definition with a working test is real progress in a field rich in claims and poor in standards. It gives geneticists a sharper tool for finding where lifestyle and inheritance truly combine.
plos-pone-0004678:
Richard Gregory and colleagues built a shared gauge of climate harm to European birds for PLOS ONE in 2009. Fast climate change is a threat to wildlife across the world. Much proof shows that recent shifts have already moved plant and animal numbers, but no single gauge summed up the harm.

The team used long term counts of bird numbers across wide areas. From those counts they built one clear sign of change that can be tracked year by year. A shared gauge helps leaders see trends at a glance. It also helps the public judge if steps to curb warming are working.
plos-pone-0004778:
Ambreen Ansari and colleagues studied cytokine gene variants across the range of tuberculosis in Pakistani patients, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Pakistan ranks among the highest burden countries for tuberculosis worldwide. Reports from other populations show varied links between cytokine gene forms and how likely TB is or how severe it becomes once infection takes hold.

Cytokines are immune signals that shape the fight against the TB bacterium. The team compared gene forms across clinical types in Pakistan. Local data matter, since gene effects can differ by population. The results may help predict severe disease. The results give future studies a clearer base for comparison and follow up.
plos-pone-0004878:
Rami Mahdi and Eric Rouchka presented RBF-TSS for identification of copying start sites using radial basis networks, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Accurate identification of promoter regions and copying start sites in genomic DNA allows complete knowledge of gene structure and control. Many published methods achieved high accuracy, and the new method combines radial basis function networks with oligonucleotide positional frequencies to locate starts in human sequences.

Machine learning captures subtle sequence signals around starts. Better annotation improves all downstream gene studies. Promoter prediction remains computationally challenging. Hybrid features outperform single signals. The study gives researchers concrete leads that later work can verify and extend.
plos-pone-0004978:
Some earlier studies blamed VEGF gene variants for heart defects at birth. The results disagreed with each other. Helen Griffin and colleagues ran a comprehensive test in PLOS ONE in 2009. They examined common promoter variants in the VEGF gene. The question was whether they contribute to congenital cardiovascular malformation.

The study found no significant contribution. Genetic variation in VEGF does not meaningfully raise the risk. A negative result like this settles a disputed question. It tells gene hunters to look elsewhere. The roots of these birth defects lie in other genes or in other kinds of variation. Future studies can spend their effort more wisely.
plos-pone-0005078:
Malaria's first stop in the body is the liver. Lowering the liver burden lowers disease severity. Iana Parvanova and colleagues tested a drug strategy in PLOS ONE in 2009. They used a small molecule inhibitor of signal peptide peptidase. That enzyme helps process proteins inside cells. The parasite needs it during liver development.

The inhibitor blocked Plasmodium development in the liver. Treated animals suffered less severe malaria. The result flags a new drug target at malaria's earliest stage. Attacking the liver stage is a promising form of prevention. The study builds on the logic of gamma-secretase inhibitors. It shows a related enzyme can be drugged against the parasite.
plos-pone-0005178:
Most people in the world lack access to advanced medical care, yet mobile phones are now widespread. Laufer and Rubinsky asked in PLOS ONE in 2009 whether a phone could help sort tissues without any cut into the body. Their setup pairs the phone with simple electrical measures of tissue.

The study shows that those measures, read by classifier software on the phone, can tell tissue types apart. No sample needs to be taken from the patient. A phone-based test like this could bring basic screening to clinics with little gear, and it points to a low-cost path for remote care.
plos-pone-0005278:
After brain injury such as stroke, new neurons can wake in a region called the subventricular zone. Vergni and colleagues built a model to watch that activation, reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their system uses rat brain slices that keep cortex, zone, and striatum together.

In the slices, the team modeled ischemia, the blood loss that a stroke causes. Neuroblast activation was described through growth and movement measures. A slice model lets researchers test repair ideas quickly, before moving to whole-animal studies of stroke recovery. Brain slices stay alive for hours in a dish, so dose and time can be changed at will, which makes this shelf a fast first test for stroke drugs.
plos-pone-0005378:
Biologists often need fresh hypotheses when experiments give puzzling results. Weinreb and colleagues described a computer method for generating alternative hypotheses in PLOS ONE in 2009, built on their causal mapping tool, CMAP.

CMAP models cell and molecular processes as coarse-grained graphs of causes. From a graph, the method derives other explanations that fit the same facts. Automated brainstorming like this can rescue stalled projects by showing researchers explanations they had not considered. A tool that lists fresh options when a team is stuck can save weeks of work. It does not prove a claim, but it can point a team to the one test that will, and that is the point of good guess work in lab science.
plos-pone-0005478:
Meetu Seth and colleagues searched for signs of hidden tuberculosis in cattle, in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Bovine tuberculosis is common in herds in many lands, though rare in the United States. Tests are muddied there by a related germ that infects many cattle without causing the same disease.

The team looked for blood markers that appear when cattle carry the tuberculosis germ quietly. A marker that can tell the two germs apart would let vets find infected herds sooner. Better detection protects both farm income and the people who drink milk or handle cattle.
plos-pone-0005578:
Valsala Haridas and co-authors studied a plant compound and a cancer signal in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Avicins are plant compounds that can trigger death in cancer cells and calm inflammation. They work in part by chemically altering key proteins.

The team studied one avicin's effect on Stat3, a protein that promotes growth in many cancers. The compound removed an activating tag from Stat3 by acting on both the enzymes that add the tag and those that remove it. That two-sided action makes the compound a useful probe and a possible drug lead.
plos-pone-0005678:
Changsong Yang and co-authors filmed the moving edge of cells in 2009 to see how thin spikes called filopodia push out. A crawling cell extends its front edge, and both the outer membrane and the actin skeleton inside must change in step. Which one leads was not clear.

The team tracked membrane shape and actin fibers at the same time. Their work weighs two views: that growing actin rods push the membrane out, or that the membrane moves first and actin follows. Settling that order matters for knowing how cells crawl, heal wounds, and, in cancer, spread. The study gives close, timed views of both parts at once.
plos-pone-0005778:
David Dreyfus argued in 2009 that acquired immunity may have begun when an ancient virus-like element lodged in a genome. The RAG proteins, which shuffle antibody genes in B and T cells, act much like the cutting tools of mobile DNA. That likeness suggests the immune system's core trick was borrowed.

Dreyfus assembles evidence for a herpes-like source of that borrowed element. If right, the defense that protects us started as an invader. The hypothesis guides searches for matching sequences in early vertebrates. It is a bold claim, laid out for others to test against fossils of DNA.
plos-pone-0005878:
Liang Wang and co-authors paired two genome-wide scans in 2009 to tie microRNAs to the genes they regulate in human cells. Gene activity varies naturally between people, and much of that variation is inherited. MicroRNAs are one layer of control, but mapping their targets in real populations was new.

Using lymphoblastoid cell lines, the team correlated microRNA levels with gene expression across many individuals. Genes that fall as a microRNA rises are candidate targets, filtered by real human variation. The approach grounds predictions in data rather than sequence alone. It offers a resource for studies of disease-linked expression changes.
plos-pone-0005978:
Low oxygen over weeks strains both the heart and the lungs, but not in the same way. Sally Vitali, Alex Mitsialis, Olin Liang and colleagues teased those effects apart in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies mice lacking heme oxygenase-1, an enzyme switched on by low oxygen in heart and vessel cells, and the products that enzyme makes.

Mice without the enzyme fare worse under long low oxygen, with lung pressure rising and the right side of the heart harmed. Yet the enzyme's products pull in divergent directions in heart and lung. That split warns that a treatment helping one organ may burden the other, a key point for lung-heart disease care.
plos-pone-0006078:
Sleep is when the cortex reshapes itself around the day's experience. Sara Aton, Julie Seibt, Michelle Dumoulin and colleagues asked in 2009 whether a common sleep drug blocks that reshaping. Their PLOS ONE paper studies trazodone, a sedating antidepressant that works through monoamine receptors, unlike the GABA-targeting sleep drugs already known to impair sleep-dependent plasticity.

The title gives the answer: trazodone impairs the cortical plasticity that sleep should bring. A drug taken for sleep that blunts sleep's brain benefit is a poor bargain for some patients. The finding widens the caution beyond one drug class and gives prescribers a reason to weigh brain effects, not just hours slept.
plos-pone-0006178:
Sea cucumbers lack the neat immune organs that backboned animals have, yet their guts still answer attacks. Francisco Ramirez-Gomez and colleagues studied gut tissue in the sea cucumber Holothuria glaberrima for a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They used a bacterial product called LPS, a common trigger, to switch the tissue's defences on.

The team catalogued which genes turned on in the gut after the trigger. The results show that organs not built for defence can still join the immune response. That finding widens the picture of immunity in animals without backbones. It may also help explain how sea cucumbers heal and regrow gut tissue so well.
plos-pone-0006278:
The tissue around a tumor usually helps it grow, but fat tissue cells may do the opposite. Beatrice Cousin and colleagues tested adult stromal cells from human fat against pancreatic cancer in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Normal tissue balance depends on constant talk between epithelial cells and their surroundings; cancer breaks that balance.

The fat-derived cells provoked pancreatic cancer cell death both in dishes and in living animals. A cell type from ordinary body fat thus shows anti-tumor action. The finding suggests a possible cell-based treatment route for a hard cancer. It also reframes how the tumor environment can be used against itself.
plos-pone-0006378:
The rails inside cells, called microtubules, are built and taken apart all through the life of a cell. Bernard Piette and his team built a heat and energy model of that build and break cycle in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. These rails are key to two big tasks: pulling gene bundles apart and the last split of a cell in two.

The model ties the speed of growth to the energy the parts carry. It shows which facts set how fast a rail grows or falls apart. Such rules help make sense of the wild swings seen under the microscope. They also guide drugs that freeze the rails to stop cancer growth.
plos-pone-0006478:
Robert Bradley and co-authors modeled the evolution of non-coding RNAs in fruit flies for PLOS ONE in 2009. Non-coding RNAs are RNA molecules that work without becoming proteins. Finding their genes in a genome is hard, since they leave faint signals. The team benchmarked prediction methods that use evolutionary grammar models.

They experimented with eight models of structural evolution and two prediction programs. Benchmarks show which model best balances finding real genes against false alarms. Better prediction expands the known RNA catalog in Drosophila, a key model species. The lessons also apply to gene hunting in other animals.
plos-pone-0006578:
Kennedy Matsagas, David Lim, Marc Horwitz, and colleagues tested long-term drug effects in fruit flies for PLOS ONE in 2009. Small invertebrate animals, such as nematodes and fruit flies, are increasingly used to test candidate drugs. They serve both specific therapeutic purposes and long-term safety testing. The team examined functional side-effects of stimulants and sedatives in Drosophila melanogaster.

Long-term effects are hard to study in short-lived patients trials, but flies live fast. Functional readouts show whether behavior and health suffer over time. The work supports flies as an early screen for drug safety. It may flag problems before mammalian testing.
plos-pone-0006678:
Darryll D. Dudley, Hong-Cheng Wang, and Xiao-Hong Sun examined a protein called Hes1 in PLOS ONE in 2009. Hes1 belongs to a family of proteins switched on by Notch signaling. These proteins repress transcription, turning other genes down. Mice lacking Hes1 had hinted that it matters for normal development. The authors asked what happens when Hes1 stays active in T cells.

Their work shows Hes1 can strengthen T cell lymphomagenesis, the formation of T cell lymphoma. It does so by raising activity in a subset of Notch target genes. That links a single repressor protein to cancer growth in immune cells. The study clarifies how Notch signaling can tip toward malignancy. It may help explain some T cell cancers in people.
plos-pone-0006778:
Elizabeth M. Goebel, Xuqing Zhang, and Eric T. Harvill tested cross-protection between two Bordetella bacteria in mice in PLOS ONE in 2009. One species, B. bronchiseptica, infects many mammals and spreads efficiently. It is rarely seen in humans. The other, B. pertussis, causes whooping cough in people. It appears specialized for the human host.

Mice were infected with or vaccinated against B. pertussis. They were then challenged with B. bronchiseptica. Prior exposure substantially protected them, as the title reports. Shared antigens likely explain the protection. The result shows immunity crosses between these related bacteria. It may inform vaccine designs that borrow protection across species lines.
plos-pone-0006878:
Leticia Ochoa-Ochoa and her team weighed two ways to guard land for Mexico's frogs and toads in PLOS ONE in 2009. Land guard plans tend to count just state-run parks. Towns and land owners now guard land in their own ways too. Those grass-roots acts add up to a real force for wild life. Mexico's frogs and toads are rich in kinds and much at risk.

The team set state parks next to grass-roots guard work. They asked how much frog and toad safety each one brings. Town-held land may shield kinds and homes the state parks miss. Put side by side, the two can close gaps that each leaves on its own. Plans should count town-held land with full weight.
plos-pone-0006978:
Yubo Hou and Senjie Lin compared genome sizes across life forms in PLOS ONE in 2009. Predicting how many genes an unsequenced genome holds is a prized skill. It is especially wanted for dinoflagellates, whose huge genomes resist sequencing. The pair used fully sequenced genomes from many branches of life as their base.

They found the link between gene number and genome size differs by group. Eukaryotes follow one pattern, and non-eukaryotes another. Applying the right pattern gave gene counts for dinoflagellate genomes. Those estimates guide genome projects before costly sequencing begins.
plos-pone-0007078:
Caroline Savage and Andrew Vickers audited data sharing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many journals require authors to share their data with other researchers. Authors can deposit data publicly or send it on request. These rules are explicit but had barely been tested. The pair checked authors publishing in PLoS journals.

They asked how well authors actually complied with sharing policies. Empirical checks matter because shared data underpins replication. If requests quietly fail, published findings rest on weaker ground. Their audit gave editors rare hard numbers on a policy most journals simply assume works.
plos-pone-0007178:
Jin Hu, Ola Winqvist, Amilcar Flores-Morales, and colleagues studied human immune cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Their focus is dendritic cells, which show foreign material to other immune cells. Labs can grow these cells from blood monocytes and then mature them with a bacterial signal called LPS.

The authors ask how a regulator protein named SOCS2 changes that maturation step. They follow human monocyte-derived dendritic cells as they respond to LPS. Their findings add detail to how the immune system tunes its first response to bacterial infection and inflammation.
plos-pone-0007278:
Paul van Donkelaar, Yu Lin, and David Hewlett studied eye movement planning in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Saccades are rapid eye movements that align central vision with objects of interest. Children often make quick saccades that are poorly planned and fall short of their target, the authors had shown.

The authors test adults on a gap saccade task. They examine frontal oculomotor areas in the cortex, the brain regions that plan eye movements. They report asymmetric contributions from the two sides of the brain. Their work clarifies how the brain plans fast, accurate gaze shifts.
plos-pone-0007378:
Yan Ropert-Coudert, Lisa Brooks, Maki Yamamoto, and colleagues measured koala heart responses to tourists in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Koalas operate on a tight energy budget. They may not show behavioral avoidance even when stressed, because moving costs energy they cannot spare on their low-nutrition eucalyptus diet.

The authors investigate physiological responses of captive koalas at a conservation centre. They record ECG, the heart's electrical signal, as tourists approach. Their preliminary study tests whether hearts reveal stress that behavior hides. Wildlife centres can use such measures to judge visitor distances and handling rules.
plos-pone-0007478:
Anne Beghin and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on a small molecular switch protein called Arl2 and its role in breast cancer. Earlier work showed Arl2 levels affect how breast tumor cells divide and how their internal skeleton behaves. The open question was whether Arl2 changes how aggressive tumors become in a living body. The team tested that in mice lacking immune defenses.

They grew two different human breast tumors in the mice, with Arl2 levels raised or lowered. Shifting Arl2 changed how aggressively the tumors behaved. That moves Arl2 from a cell-culture curiosity to a driver of tumor character in vivo. A switch that controls aggressiveness is a possible drug target. It is also a candidate marker for judging how dangerous a tumor may be.
plos-pone-0007578:
Erik Hill and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on cocaine methiodide, a charged variant of cocaine. Unlike cocaine itself, this analog cannot cross the blood-brain barrier. Researchers therefore use it to study the drug's actions on the body alone. Yet its strength at cocaine's main molecular targets had never been pinned down clearly. The team measured those potencies in mice.

They determined how strongly the analog hits each major target, including the transporters cocaine is known to block. Firm numbers let researchers interpret older experiments with confidence. They also sharpen new ones that separate body effects from brain effects. Cocaine's harms to the heart and vessels happen outside the brain, so the distinction matters. The study is measurement work, the kind that makes other experiments trustworthy.
plos-pone-0007678:
Eduardo Altmann, Janet Pierrehumbert and Adilson Motter published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on the timing of words in text. Word counts follow a famous rule: a few words appear often, and most appear rarely. The authors asked a different question, about when words show up.

They tracked bursts, when a word appears many times in a short span, and lulls, when it fades from use. They found that these timing patterns follow scaling laws, much like patterns in nature. The work hints that the rhythm of language carries information that plain counts miss.
plos-pone-0007778:
Thomas Ioerger and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It reads the genomes of drug-resistant TB strains from KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. That region had suffered an outbreak of extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis. The outbreak strains belong to the highly virulent KZN family.

The team sequenced strains that resist many drugs, and some that resist nearly all. Comparing their genomes shows how resistance evolved step by step. It also reveals which mutations matter most. Genome clues like these help labs track dangerous strains. They can also guide the search for drugs that still work.
plos-pone-0007878:
Nian Xiong and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It presents a rat model meant to mirror Parkinson's disease more faithfully. A good animal model could reveal what causes the disease. It could also speed the testing of new medicines.

Existing toxin-based models fail to copy the main clinical features. They also miss the disease's slow pathology. The team infused rotenone precisely into rat brains using stereotaxic guidance. They report the model is reliable for research use. A model that behaves like the human disease makes drug screening far more meaningful.
plos-pone-0007978:
Apratim Mitra and colleagues used chip data to compare genomes within a species, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their tool was array-based comparative genomic hybridization, which counts how many copies of each DNA stretch a sample holds. Such copy shifts are a large source of variety.

The team built a way to read those shifts and draw family ties from them. Copy patterns can show how alike two samples are and how groups split over time. The method turns a tool made for disease work into one for basic questions about variety and kinship.
plos-pone-0008078:
Aneta Kotevski and colleagues reported a ghost gene found on mouse chromosome 7 in PLOS ONE in 2009. The look-alike mimics XIAP, a real gene that blocks the cell death program and juggles many partners. Genome scans had flagged the copy as if it were a second working gene.

Close reading showed the copy is a pseudogene, a worn fossil that makes no working protein. Naming it as a fossil matters. Without the label, labs could waste years chasing a gene that does nothing, or misread tests that pick up its echo.
plos-pone-0008178:
Felix Wussow, Helmut Fickenscher, and B. Karsten Tischer described a lab method in PLOS ONE in 2009 for handling cloned herpesvirus genomes. Scientists often clone large viral genomes inside bacteria using bacterial artificial chromosomes, or BACs. These carriers help build test viruses and targeting tools. A cloning carrier must later be removed cleanly.

The team used Red-mediated transposition to move and finally release the mini-F vector part of the clone. Red-based methods let researchers edit BACs inside Escherichia coli with care. A clean final release leaves the infectious viral genome free of carrier parts. That makes the clone safer and more exact for later study.
plos-pone-0008278:
Inés Horovitz, Thomas Martin, and Jonathan Bloch described early marsupial skulls in PLOS ONE in 2009. The early evolution of living marsupials is poorly understood. Early members of the group are known almost only from jaws and teeth. That gap limits knowledge of how living marsupials are related. It also clouds the origin of opossums.

New cranial material fills part of that gap. Skulls reveal far more about diet, senses, and kinship than teeth alone. The authors used the anatomy to place early marsupials on the family tree. Their work clarifies where opossums came from.
plos-pone-0008378:
Song Yang and Philip E. Bourne traced protein domain history in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. Protein structural domains are evolutionary units of proteins. Their relationships can be detected over long evolutionary distances. Domain history includes origins, loss, transfer, duplication, and new combinations. Viewing that history through species phylogeny was the authors' approach.

They mapped how domains changed as species diverged. Gains and losses of domains mark key steps in protein evolution. That view helps explain how new protein functions arise. It also informs the classification of proteins across all life.
plos-pone-0008478:
Raghavan Madhavan and co-authors study a protein at nerve-muscle junctions in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. At those junctions, clusters of acetylcholine receptors receive nerve signals. Clustering depends on a muscle receptor called MuSK. A nerve protein called agrin switches MuSK on. That switch starts a chain of signals inside the muscle cell. The team ask where cortactin fits in that chain.

Cortactin helps organize the cell skeleton near the membrane. The authors test if it is needed for receptor clusters to form. Their results place cortactin in the clustering process. The work adds a step to how synapses between nerve and muscle are built.
plos-pone-0008578:
Markus Hilty and co-authors compare airway germs in asthma in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. A rich germ environment in infancy protects against asthma. Yet infections also trigger asthma attacks. The team compare airway microbiota in adults with asthma. They also study patients with COPD, a related lung disease, and healthy controls. Samples come from three levels of the airways.

They find the microbial communities in asthmatic airways are disordered. The mix of germs differs from that in healthy airways. Such disorder may sustain inflammation even without a clear infection. The work shifts asthma research toward the whole airway community, not single germs.
plos-pone-0008678:
Toshio Kodama, Kazuyoshi Gotoh, Hirotaka Hiyoshi, and coworkers studied a germ that spoils seafood meals. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article looks at Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a cause of food poisoning around the world. Much of its harm comes from one stretch of DNA called Vp-PAI. That stretch holds toxin genes and a needle-like system for injecting proteins.

The team asked which switches turn those island genes on or off. They singled out two regulator proteins that help drive gut toxicity. Blocking such switches could weaken the germ without killing it outright. The work gives drug hunters a clearer picture of how this pathogen causes illness.
plos-pone-0008778:
Stuart Wilson, Judith Law, Ben Mitchinson, and colleagues modeled how rat brains map whisker movement. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A recent experiment found pinwheel patterns in the rat barrel cortex. Each pinwheel sorts whisker pushes by direction. The layout recalls maps seen in visual brain areas. How such a map builds itself during development was unknown.

The model grew maps from simple activity-based rules. Simulated maps matched the pinwheel layout seen in real brains. Self-organization may thus explain the pattern without detailed wiring instructions. The work links touch maps in rats to broader rules of brain development.
plos-pone-0008878:
Charles Willis, Brad Ruhfel, Richard Primack, and colleagues used Henry David Thoreau's old plant records to judge invasion success. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Non-native plants often outcompete local ones as climate warms. Thoreau catalogued Concord's flora in the 1850s with unusual care. Modern surveys of the same woods show which species won or lost. Climate response was the suspected edge.

Plants that shifted their flowering with warming fared best, and non-natives shifted more. That favorable response explains much of the invaders' success. The finding warns that warming tilts plant contests toward newcomers. Historical records prove priceless for such century-scale tests.
plos-pone-0008978:
Claudia Kruger and Claudia Kappen studied mice carrying extra copies of two body-plan genes, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hox genes tell a growing embryo where body parts belong. They also guide cartilage cells as they mature into the tissue that precedes bone. Too much Hoxc8 or Hoxd4 activity badly deforms cartilage in these mice.

The pair measured which cartilage development genes changed under the overdose. Genes that cartilage cells need for orderly growth shifted up or down. The pattern helps explain why the animals' skeletons form wrongly. It also shows how a small dosing error in one gene can ripple across a whole tissue.
plos-pone-0009078:
Pradeep Gupta, Shihui Liu, and Stephen Leppla profiled a mutant hamster cell that shrugs off bacterial toxins, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chinese hamster ovary cells are workhorses of cell biology labs. The mutant was found by inserting retroviruses to break genes at random. It survived several toxins that normally poison cells by tagging proteins.

The resistance traced to a fault in elongation factor-2. That factor is a core part of the cell's protein-building machinery. The toxins attack exactly that factor, so breaking it first blocks them. Mutants like this reveal which cell parts a toxin truly needs.
plos-pone-0009178:
Akira Yamasaki and co-authors reported this cell biology study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Their subject is asthma, a disease where airways swell and tighten. Earlier work had linked a signaling protein called IL-9 to the inflammation behind allergic asthma. The team asked how IL-9 acts on the muscle cells that line the airways.

Working with human airway smooth muscle cells, they traced what IL-9 switches on inside the cell. They found that IL-9 raises production of CCL11, a chemical that draws in allergy-related immune cells. The signal runs through a relay protein called STAT3. That pathway helps explain how IL-9 may feed the long-term airway changes seen in asthma.
plos-pone-0009278:
Elizabeth Selig and John Bruno published this ocean study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Reef-building corals are declining worldwide under pressure from human activity. Coral reefs hold great value for wildlife, coasts, and people, so their loss is a global concern. Marine protected areas, where fishing and other uses are limited, are a leading tool to save them.

The authors analyzed evidence from protected areas around the world. They asked whether protection actually slows or prevents coral loss inside the reserves. A global verdict matters because reserves are costly and politically hard to create. Their answer helps conservation groups spend that effort where it works.
plos-pone-0009378:
Maria Christina Shina and co-authors published this slime mold study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dictyostelium is an amoeba that moves and feeds as a single cell. Its genome carries several Sec7 genes, which make proteins that switch other proteins on. Those switch proteins fall into three families found across complex life.

The team characterized a Dictyostelium member of the cytohesin family. Cytohesins were known from animals, where they help run cell traffic and signaling. Finding and describing the amoeba's version shows how far back this family reaches. It also gives a simple organism in which to study what cytohesins do.
plos-pone-0009478:
Francisco Quintana and co-authors looked at immune control in zebrafish in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fish, like people, build a wide set of immune receivers by shuffling gene parts. That power brings a risk: some receivers may attack the body's own tissues. In mammals, regulatory T cells that carry Foxp3 keep that risk in check.

The team found a like system at work in zebrafish. These fish are among the oldest backboned animals with this kind of immunity. So the peacekeeping role of Foxp3 cells is very old. The finding shows that immune self control has deep evolutionary roots.
plos-pone-0009578:
Mikael Lindstrom and Monica Nister silenced a ribosome part in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ribosomes build the cell's proteins. When their work is disturbed, the tumor guard p53 often wakes and stops growth. A small set of ribosome proteins can trigger that alarm. The team turned off ribosomal protein S9 in cultured cells and watched what followed.

Silencing S9 set off a wide set of cell responses tied to p53. Cancer cell growth slowed as a result. The work shows how closely protein making is tied to tumor defense. A ribosome part can thus be a weak point that future cancer research may exploit.
plos-pone-0009678:
Zebrafish are small striped fish that labs around the world use to study hormones and development. In 2010, Gayathri Chandrasekar and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE how much estrogen receptor zebrafish carry at two life stages. They compared embryos with adult fish after dosing with natural and lab-made chemicals that bind these receptors.

Estrogen receptors are proteins that let cells respond to estrogen and similar chemicals in water. Counting them before and after exposure gives a baseline for a widely used test animal. The results help researchers judge how estrogen-like pollutants may affect fish while they are still growing.
plos-pone-0009878:
Finding where transcription factors bind DNA is a core task in genomics. Xiang Zhou and colleagues approached that prediction from systems biology, using whole-network thinking. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Transcription factors are the proteins that switch genes on and off.

A binding site is a short DNA stretch a factor grips to control a gene. Systems biology adds context, like which genes work together, to raw sequence clues. Better predictions save lab time and sharpen gene maps. The approach treats binding as part of a living network, not a lone pattern.
plos-pone-0009978:
Long life, strong immunity, and stress resistance may rise and fall together in tiny worms. Francis Amrit, Claudia Boehnisch, and Robin May measured how those traits covary. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The worms live only a few weeks, so aging is quick to study.

Phenotypic covariance means two traits change together across individuals. The animals were Caenorhabditis nematodes, worms widely used in aging research. If the traits trade off, breeding for one may cost another. Shared roots would mean one pathway steers aging, defense, and toughness together.
plos-pone-0010078:
The authors were Ryan Kitko, Jessica Wilks, Gian Garduque, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study asked how E. coli bacteria keep their inner acidity steady. Cells use many tricks for that job, including chemical breakdown and ion flows across the membrane. Potassium flow is a known contributor, but how it compensates for acid stress was unclear.

The team tested osmolytes, small molecules that protect cells from water stress. They found these molecules also contribute to pH balance in E. coli. The result links two survival systems that were often studied apart.
plos-pone-0010178:
Pascal Feunou, Julie Bertout, and Camille Locht tested a new whooping cough vaccine in mice in 2010. Despite wide vaccine use, whooping cough still kills many children around the world each year. Two vaccine types exist, older whole-cell and newer acellular forms. Newer ones cause fewer reactions, yet protection can fade over time.

Their candidate was a live, weakened pertussis vaccine given to mice. It raised protection through both T cells and B cells, the two arms of immune memory. It also cross-protected against parapertussis, a related illness. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE.
plos-pone-0010278:
Ryuji Machida and Atsushi Tsuda compared plankton species by their genes in a 2010 study. Six species of Neocalanus copepods, tiny crustaceans, inhabit the world's oceans. Three species and two form variants in the North Pacific form one related group. Their PLOS ONE paper used four gene sequences, from mitochondria and the nucleus, to measure dissimilarity.

Comparing several genes guards against being misled by any single one. Their distances test whether the named species and forms are truly distinct. Copepods anchor ocean food webs, so their true diversity matters for ecology.
plos-pone-0010378:
Tamara Romanuk and colleagues tested whether stress changes how variety steadies nature, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Diverse communities of species often weather change better than poor ones. Stress, though, might weaken or strengthen that link. The team used shrinking water volume as the stress in small aquatic systems. They then watched whether more diverse setups stayed more stable.

Across the stress gradient, the positive link between variety and stability held up. That is not a given; many expected stress to break the pattern. Living variety thus seems to insure communities even under strain. The finding supports protecting diversity before hard times arrive. Once a stress hits, the insurance is already either bought or lost.
plos-pone-0010478:
Sujit Dutta and Katrin Rittinger mapped how an enzyme that makes reactive oxygen is switched on and off for PLOS ONE in 2010. Reactive oxygen species fight germs but also carry signals inside cells. Too much damages tissue, so their sources are tightly governed. The enzyme component NOXO1 is one such source's organizer. The team studied its reversible partnerships with two other proteins.

NOXO1 binds one partner, p22phox, and another, NOXA1, in ways that can be undone. Those reversible contacts tune the enzyme's activity up or down. Detailed maps of such contacts help design drugs that adjust oxygen signaling. The work is basic biochemistry with wide medical echoes. It shows control by association, not just by amount.
plos-pone-0010578:
Lei Liu and colleagues explored how a drug slows moving cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The drug was rapamycin, already known to block a growth pathway inside cells. The signal they studied was IGF-1, which normally urges cells to crawl and spread.

Cell experiments showed rapamycin blunted the movement that IGF-1 provokes. The effect ran through a second protein, PP2A, which helps switch other proteins off. Tracing that chain explains part of how rapamycin acts. It also hints at ways to limit the spread of tumor cells, which depend on similar movement signals.
plos-pone-0010678:
Shuzhen Sim and George Dimopoulos studied how dengue virus quiets mosquito defenses, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Dengue spreads when Aedes aegypti mosquitoes bite people. The virus must first live and grow inside the mosquito, whose immune system fights back with its own gene responses.

In infected mosquito cells, many defense genes failed to switch on as they should. The virus seemed to damp the response rather than merely dodge it. That damping helps the virus build up numbers before the mosquito's next bite. Knowing which defenses get muted suggests ways to breed or engineer mosquitoes that resist dengue from within.
plos-pone-0010778:
Adeel Safdar and colleagues studied the energy centers of muscle in inactive older adults, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Muscle mass melts away with age, a process called sarcopenia. Faulty mitochondria, the cell's energy centers, are often blamed. What was unclear is whether a sedentary life, rather than age itself, drives much of that fault.

Muscle samples from sedentary older adults showed disordered mitochondrial upkeep. The balance between making new mitochondria and clearing worn ones had slipped.
